391. ID: 240
   Year: 2021
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Technical University of Denmark, Aalborg University
   Statement: How to expand offshore energy islands
Preparations for the energy islands are in full swing, with the aim of establishing operations by 2033 at the latest. However, once they are built, they will exist for a much longer time and be able to handle significantly larger electricity production based on offshore wind and possibly also the electricity consumption in power-to-gas plants. The energy island in the North Sea will be built for 3 GW, but must
be designed to be expandable to 10 GW and potentially be connected to other islands to form a
European offshore DC grid.
The energy islands therefore represent a significant change in the paradigm of how offshore connections have been built so far. Today, offshore connections are built between individual production units (a
wind farm or an oil/gas platform) and an entry point to the energy system. There is no experience
with reinforcing or modifying offshore connections for expansion once they are in operation.
The scale of this challenge becomes clear when you look at how quickly technology is developing in areas such as power electronics. The initial design must be scalable, i.e. able to be expanded with more devices with their own control, without the need for extensive retrofitting or major design changes. At all stages, the technology chosen must allow for a high degree of freedom and not limit future expansion with more intelligent solutions, while ensuring a high degree of robustness. Another critical challenge is ensuring that system components can “talk” to each other and work together. This is called interoperability*. There will be a significant number of power electronic devices on
offshore energy islands – either as inverters in wind turbines or as large HVDC converters. Power electronic converters are versatile and flexible devices with complex and advanced control algorithms. Operationally, converters are (almost) exclusively defined by their control (software) rather than by their physical characteristics (hardware), which primarily define the converters’ limitations. In their final form, the offshore energy islands’ electrical system will include multiple wind farms and HVDC converters from multiple manufacturers, and their control systems will be specific and proprietary to each supplier.
Therefore, a system (wind farm) or a component (HVDC converter) must be able to work effectively with other systems and/or components from another supplier. The challenge here is to develop a process that ensures interoperability without requiring full disclosure of the detailed converter control from the manufacturers. And this must be done knowing that the converter control software (and hardware technology) of 2030 will likely be significantly different from what is available today.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

519. ID: 5545
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: I have approved Energinet's application for the "Energiø Bornholm Electrical Infrastructure" project. This project aims to establish the necessary collective transmission network and associated electrical facilities to connect the Energy Island of Bornholm to Denmark's electricity transmission grid. Specifically, it includes a 245 km direct current connection between Bornholm and Zealand and the construction of two 400 kV stations with converter facilities on Bornholm and Zealand.

The approval follows thorough technical reviews and political agreements, including the expansion of Energiø Bornholm's capacity from 2 GW to 3 GW as of the August 2022 political supplementary agreement, and a July 2022 agreement with Germany for their connection to the Energy Island via the German TSO, 50Hertz. Negotiations on the allocation of ownership, costs, and revenues between Energinet and 50Hertz are ongoing.

As per preliminary assessments, the project's construction budget for Energinet has been reduced from DKK 16.9 billion to approximately DKK 13.9 billion, excluding risk costs, due to co-financing principles established in the agreement with Germany. Operating costs have similarly been projected to decrease from DKK 121 million to DKK 114 million annually.

The project must be executed as outlined in the submitted materials, adhering to the specified technical solutions and assumptions within Energinet’s business case. Any significant changes to the project must be promptly reported to the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities for separate approval.

520. ID: 4043
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Council on Climate Change
   Statement: Offshore wind turbines are the key driver that can provide sufficient amounts of green electricity.

By 2030, the total capacity of wind turbines in Denmark is planned to increase from 2.3 gigawatts this year to 5.8 gigawatts by 2030. However, several large parks—such as Thor and Hesselø—will not be ready for 5-8 years.

If we are to see more green electricity in our power outlets, I believe the political parties should accelerate the large offshore wind projects already agreed upon at Christiansborg.

Additionally, there are plans for a massive so-called energy island in the North Sea, which is set to have a capacity of three gigawatts by 2033, expanding to 10 gigawatts by 2040. I also believe this should be expedited.

Onshore wind turbines are much faster to construct compared to large offshore wind farms, which take many years to build.

However, onshore wind farms often face significant resistance from local residents in the areas where energy companies, farmers, and others want to install turbines.

For this reason, the Danish Energy Agency expects only a 20% increase in onshore wind turbines over the next eight years, according to a response to the Climate Committee in Parliament.

Concerns for nature also often clash with plans for more onshore wind turbines. In North Jutland, Denmark's largest onshore wind farm at Thorup-Sletten was delayed because, according to critics, the turbines posed a threat to several animal species, including the birds of prey, the marsh harrier and the hen harrier.

I believe the state should play a bigger role and ensure that more municipalities participate in building wind turbines.

The risks with the greatest potential economic impact on the project include the following:  
1. **Technical Risks**: Challenges related to the development of HVDC standards, technology, and integration with the Bornholm electricity system.  
2. **Market Conditions**: Unforeseen market conditions and overheating, partly due to developments in Ukraine.

4. **Ownership Changes**: Potential changes in the ownership distribution of the cable connecting to Germany.

540. ID: 2210
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: LinkedIn user
   Statement: Here is a challenge. I completely agree that the focus of the decision must be the justification, especially because it is not a harbor facility as such.

But the question of zoning status for the areas that arise from the sea territory, naturally or by reclamation, must be a misunderstanding in the decision. That is, "that the municipality has erroneously assumed that the new land areas from the inclusion of sea territory become part of the coastal part of the urban zone and not part of the coastal zone."

From a corrected decision in a 2020 appeal case regarding Faxe Municipality's final adoption of municipal plan supplement no. 13 and local plan no. 300-46, it appears that:

"The Planning Appeals Board does not find it contrary to the Planning Act to adopt planning for a land area that arises after the reclamation of the area following the necessary permits, including from the Coastal Directorate. Thus, there may be a planning need to adopt the necessary planning for the use of the areas in question before reclamation is possibly permitted and carried out. The overall planning purpose behind the intended project can thus be subjected to public debate and any resulting adjustments before concrete decisions are made on whether reclamation can take place for the purpose(s) intended through planning for the area. It is also quite common in other contexts to plan before concrete decisions are made on, for example, exemptions from the Nature Protection Act and the like. It is also not contrary to the Planning Act to adopt planning for an area that is expected to arise naturally. However, the planning will not have an effect on, for example, citizens and developers until the areas in question have actually become land areas. If the areas are re-established and become water areas again at some point, the plan will no longer have an effect on the area in question."

It is hard to imagine that the status of the area reclaimed within an existing local plan should be treated as a rural zone if it is planned as an urban zone and thus will be part of the coastal part of the urban zone when reclaimed.

But I could easily have misunderstood it myself, so yes, Sune Porse Carlsen, I think that a proper guideline on this would probably be a good idea.

541. ID: 2205
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: LinkedIn user
   Statement: New Energy Island at the Harbor on Masnedø

Vordingborg Municipality adopts Supplement 19 to the municipal plan and local plan H 17.03.01. The new planning basis aims to enable an energy island with solar panel installations northwest of Masnedø. The energy island will be connected to Masnedø when the existing harbor is expanded in accordance with the already applicable local plan H 17.01.03.

A resident outside the planning area complains to the Planning Appeals Board about the local plan, and the board annuls the local plan: The municipality does not sufficiently justify why a solar panel installation should be located near the coast or in connection with the existing harbor.

This is a significant legal deficiency, according to the Planning Appeals Board. Planning within the coastal zone requires justification. This is stated in Section 5b of the Planning Act. Only in very special cases can planning for the inclusion of sea territory be considered.

Reclaimed Sea Territory Does Not Become Urban Zone

Supplement 19 to the municipal plan and local plan H 17.03.01 transfers the new energy island to the urban zone. This plays a crucial role for the Planning Appeals Board: "The board emphasizes that the municipality has erroneously assumed that the new land areas from the inclusion of sea territory become part of the coastal part of the urban zone and not part of the coastal zone."

I do not understand this reasoning for the board's decision. According to Section 5b of the Planning Act, a municipality may transfer an area within the coastal zone to the urban zone if a coastal location can be justified in terms of planning or functionality. Therefore, it must be the justification that is the focus, and not whether the municipality includes an area in the urban zone or not.

557. ID: 3819
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ulrik Stridsbaek
   Statement: There is currently one hybrid cable in operation in Europe, connecting several wind farms in the Baltic Sea to both Denmark and Germany. This project is operated by Energinet and German grid operator 50Hertz, of which Elia owns 80%. Hybrid projects combine generation and transmission elements and connect two or more markets, unlike traditional offshore wind farms that send power to shore via individual cables to a single country.

The big problem is that all parties must have the incentive to join the development of hybrid projects, and that is not currently the case. Current regulation does not allow for the necessary sharing of costs and revenue that would incentivize all parties to invest. Despite this, Ørsted, which has built roughly a quarter of the world's wind farms at sea, sees hybrid projects as crucial to unlocking offshore wind's future potential. We think that hybrids can be a huge saving of time, money, and hassle.

The focus on projects like the North Sea Energy Island, which hinge on technologies that do not yet exist, such as effective Power-to-X solutions, distracts from viable and immediate solutions. These projects entail massive costs, including the construction of an expanded energy grid to transport energy from the North Sea, costs that are comparable to or exceed those of the energy island itself.  

Existing technologies, like renovating wind turbines to improve efficiency and installing solar panels on existing rooftops, offer practical and effective pathways to achieve Denmark’s climate goals without additional investments in the monopolized energy grid or further disruption to natural environments. These solutions are available today and do not require speculative developments or high-risk financial commitments.  

Relying on misleading news about speculative technological breakthroughs, such as solar panels that allegedly work in the dark, detracts from addressing proven solutions. For example, claims about night-functioning solar panels producing measurable energy are misleading, as the energy produced in this way is negligible and not scalable for commercial use.  

The promotion of green energy must prioritize solutions that ordinary people and businesses can adopt directly, such as solar panels and solar-integrated roofing. These options reduce dependence on costly grid expansions, protect nature, and save consumers money, while contributing meaningfully to the green transition. Denmark does not need extravagant projects like the North Sea Energy Island to meet its climate goals; it needs a focused, immediate deployment of proven renewable energy technologies.

568. ID: 5510
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Planning Appeals Board
   Statement: The municipality has failed to provide adequate justification for establishing a new energy island at Masnedø harbor. When planning within the coastal proximity zone, there must be specific planning or functional reasons - especially for projects on land that require incorporating sea territory. 

The municipality incorrectly assumed that new land areas reclaimed from sea territory would become part of the coastal urban zone rather than the coastal proximity zone. This is a significant legal deficiency.

For development in coastal proximity zones, clear justification is required under Section 5b of the Planning Act. The municipality has not sufficiently explained why a solar cell facility must be located near the coast or in connection with the existing harbor. Incorporation of sea territory can only be permitted in very special cases.

I am therefore overturning the local development plan based on these significant legal deficiencies. The supplementary plan 19 to the municipal plan and local plan H 17.03.01, which would transfer the new energy island to urban zone, cannot proceed without proper coastal zone justification.

584. ID: 5714
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ken'ichi Matsumoto ,  Yuko Matsumura
   Statement: We, Ken'ichi Matsumoto and Yuko Matsumura, believe that promoting renewable energy (RE) electricity in remote islands is critical due to its potential to address climate change and reduce reliance on expensive and less sustainable thermal power generation. Based on our research in Tsushima, we identified the key barriers to RE development as insufficient investment in infrastructure, such as grid capacity, and the lack of local technical expertise to maintain RE facilities. To overcome these barriers, we advocate for urgent investments in grid enhancements and the cultivation of local experts.

Our analysis reveals that promoting RE, including photovoltaic (PV) and wind power, generates economic benefits such as local employment (4.21–19.30 jobs annually within the island) and additional revenue for both the island (JPY 101.14–461.45 million/year) and external regions (JPY 212.60–977.32 million/year). While the local economic impacts may appear modest, these benefits contribute to regional development and can facilitate public acceptance of RE projects.

We recognize that conflicts between local residents and RE developers could arise during project acceleration, particularly due to potential environmental concerns like impacts on landscapes and ecosystems. To address this, we emphasize the need for proactive dialogue with residents to build consensus and implement precautionary measures.

Additionally, remote islands without mainland grid connections require investments in energy storage systems to stabilize the variable capacities of PV and wind power. Given the high costs of thermal power plants and the fact that part of the energy costs for these islands is subsidized by citizens elsewhere, RE adoption is not only more sustainable but also economically advantageous for both local and external communities. Future research should explore the socioeconomic impacts of expanded RE penetration alongside energy storage systems to further inform these initiatives.

626. ID: 2534
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: TenneT
   Statement: TenneT believes that the proposed Power Hub on Dogger Bank is a revolutionary solution for integrating large volumes of offshore wind power into Europe's electricity system. This initiative involves constructing an artificial island that will act as a central hub for electrical infrastructure, eliminating the need for multiple marine platforms to connect Denmark, Germany, and the Netherlands. Power generated by wind farms will be transmitted to the island using High Voltage Alternating Current (HVAC), where it will then be converted to High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) for efficient transmission to mainland countries. TenneT emphasizes that these connections will also serve as interconnectors between nations, enhancing energy cooperation and stability. Furthermore, TenneT envisions expanding this concept to encompass the entire North Sea region, which would include the UK and Norway, both of which can contribute valuable resources for balancing renewable energy supply. This project aims to significantly lower costs associated with offshore wind energy generation while supporting Europe's transition to sustainable energy.

627. ID: 3816
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Chris Peeters
   Statement: A North Sea grid is cost-effective and helps manage production volatility because wind output varies by location but often follows a predictable pattern. Meteorological phenomena like wind tend to travel across Europe, from the Irish Sea over the North Sea to the Baltic. An energy hub at sea allows wind power to remain offshore until needed by consumers onshore. This island collects wind around it and then brings it to shore or to another hub that delivers it to the country with demand at that time. This approach prevents overloading the land grid, a common issue where Germany pays Danish wind producers to turn off turbines to avoid straining the grid.

648. ID: 2714
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Bent Kiertzner
   Statement: Mr. Bertel Maigaard, Biocirc must surely have been inspired by the young and ambitious engineer Sidenius in Henrik Pontoppidan’s masterpiece Lykke-Per. Jutland needs to be modernized in terms of energy, and while Biocirc’s methods are now more modern than those proposed by Sidenius in the book, they are just as grandiose.

I hope politicians, civil servants, and project developers read the book. There is much inspiration to be drawn from it.

Tjele Langsø could be equipped with a giant hose connected to a large heat pump, which could provide free heat to the entire surrounding area. Before that, the phosphorus- and nitrogen-rich sludge covering the lakebed—currently suffocating the lake—could be removed and sent as free fertilizer to the Horn of Africa to help combat famine there. The geese that Ulrik Wilbek is eager to see disappear could, in their deceased state, be used in biogas plants, and once the geese are gone, perhaps swans and eagles killed by wind turbine blades could replace them.

The entire population of trash fish in the lake should be fished out to improve water quality, and these fish could also be used in biogas production. This would provide employment for fishermen who have lost their livelihoods due to the oxygen depletion in Danish waters and the consequent collapse of fish stocks. And so, we could continue.

The only requirement, as with Engineer Sidenius, is to disregard trivial banalities such as economic feasibility and environmental considerations. Then everything will run smoothly.

Apart from wind turbines, biogas, and solar panels, all the other elements of the so-called energy island are still undeveloped. Nonetheless, the economics of the project are claimed to be completely under control. There might be a few hundred million kroner for the citizens of Viborg and nearly free heating, and hopefully, a little will also go to Lykke-Per. Now, that’s quite certain.

Historically, in 2012, a favorable scheme was introduced, allowing private individuals to install solar panels on their homes and produce more electricity than they consumed. The surplus electricity could be deposited into the grid and retrieved when the solar panels were not producing enough.

The scheme was politically guaranteed to last at least 20 years, and solar panels were installed everywhere. They were installed where electricity was primarily consumed, which was entirely logical. Several municipalities sensibly wanted to install solar panels on their public buildings, but such anarchy could not be tolerated, and the state began losing revenue from energy taxes.

Municipalities were then required to create a separate company for each installation, which was obviously unmanageable. With the stroke of a pen, the scheme was rendered impossible. It was simply too favorable for private individuals.

Solar panels were installed everywhere, and citizens felt engaged in the green transition. But this could not be allowed to continue, so the scheme was quickly tightened and made less favorable. People stopped installing solar panels on a large scale. All that remained was the 20-year guarantee given to the first naïve individuals who believed in the state and political promises.

The then Minister for Energy, Supply, and Climate, Lars Chr. Lilleholt of the Liberal Party, was tasked with addressing this and solved it perfectly. The guarantee was abolished, effective January 1, 2020. That was the end of that. Let that be a lesson. Never trust a used car dealer or a politician.

Now solar panel owners receive about half the price for their surplus production compared to what they pay for electricity from their supplier. At times, like in the spring of 2021, it even cost private solar panel owners money to deliver electricity to the grid. You simply cannot have production where consumption also occurs—it’s pure anarchy.

What do we do, then? Since we cannot have self-sufficient electricity production in cities or factories where the electricity is immediately consumed, we must move to the countryside. This can solve several problems. A new scheme was introduced, allowing large-scale solar panel installations on agricultural land.

A skilled farmer can earn 6,000–7,000 kroner per hectare through food production. Remember—never trust a used car dealer or a politician, but this certainly does not apply to Liberal Party politicians when large agricultural interests need to be served.

It had to be done, and done effectively. A 20–30% advantage over traditional agricultural production wasn’t enough, so the scheme was designed so that by installing solar panels on good agricultural land, the landowner earns a net return of 15,000 kroner per hectare per year, without doing anything.

Now that’s something that works. Naturally, enterprising farmers are now lining up to install solar panels on their fields. You can’t blame them; it’s a win-win situation because:

Enterprising farmers are freed from the hassle of producing food and instead receive generous rewards. That’s good Liberal Party policy.
Much valuable farmland is removed from production. Reportedly, Denmark, after Bangladesh, is the most cultivated country in the world. This quickly rectifies that.
Nitrogen emissions into surrounding waters are significantly reduced.
Finally, electricity is produced in most places where it cannot be consumed locally, but an Engineer Sidenius solution can be found for that later. Always remember—ignore trivial banalities such as economic feasibility and environmental considerations. Problems are meant to be solved.
Attentive readers may already have noticed that Danish wind turbines often stand idle under favorable wind conditions. This happens because Danish wind turbines are already shut down up to 10% of the time due to what the wind industry calls "special regulation."

It’s simply impossible to utilize the electricity produced. However, here, too, a brilliant solution has been found. The Germans control and shut down Danish wind turbines—it’s not allowed in Germany—and simultaneously pay Danish wind turbine owners full compensation for lost production. That’s genius. A true Engineer Sidenius solution.

And so, everyone in the area became happy—the landowners, the mayor, and perhaps even Lykke-Per a bit more—but that was certainly well-deserved.

Seychelles does not contribute to anthropogenic effects at the same level as developed countries because we do not overconsume or overproduce. Yet, large-scale overfishing, which is still allowed, is a more pressing issue, causing destruction to the marine food chain and increasing bycatch. Additionally, the infrastructure for solar panels and wind turbines comes with its own environmental costs. These structures require heat energy for production, which often relies on fossil fuels. Seychelles lacks sufficient land area for solar panels, and the available daylight and energy storage facilities are inadequate to ensure consistent power supply during the night or overcast days. 

The placement of wind turbines in Victoria Harbor, one of the calmest areas of Mahé, is poorly thought out. A better location would be along the ridge of Mahé, where wind reversals would have minimal impact. It’s worth noting that these turbines were donated by the UAE, a leading petroleum country. While this initiative highlights the potential for Seychelles to invest in its own renewables in the future, it also demonstrates that we are emulating the approaches of developed countries largely because it is currently fashionable.

Renewables are essential for the future, but right now, building and maintaining them in Seychelles carries a high environmental cost. If reclamation continues at this rate, we risk turning Seychelles into the 'Mud Archipelago of the Indian Ocean.' I hope that in the future, we will develop renewable solutions that are better suited to our unique location and environmental needs."

662. ID: 5516

   Statement: There appears to be a challenge here. While I agree that the focus of the decision should be on the justification, especially since this is not a harbor facility as such, I believe there's a misunderstanding in the ruling regarding the zoning status of areas emerging from territorial waters, whether naturally or through land reclamation.

The Appeals Board's corrected decision from 2020 regarding Faxe Municipality's final adoption of municipal plan supplement no. 13 and local plan no. 300-46 clearly states that planning for land areas that will emerge after filling, with necessary permits from the Coastal Authority, is legally valid. There can be a planning-related need to adopt necessary plans for these areas' use before filling is permitted and implemented. This allows the overall planning purpose to undergo public debate and potential adjustments before specific decisions about land reclamation are made.

This approach is standard practice in other contexts where planning occurs before specific decisions about exemptions from nature protection laws and similar matters. It's also legal to plan for areas expected to emerge naturally, though such planning cannot take effect for citizens and developers until the areas actually become land. If these areas are later restored to water, the plan would no longer apply.

It's difficult to imagine that a reclaimed area within an existing local plan should be treated as rural zone if it's already planned as urban zone and would thus become part of the coastal urban zone upon reclamation. However, I might be misunderstanding this myself, so I agree with Sune Porse Carlsen that proper guidance on this matter would be beneficial.

680. ID: 146
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: Assessment and Expected Decision

The Danish Energy Agency has assessed that the project is necessary. It is determined that the 1.2 GW connection from Zealand to Bornholm can accommodate the need for integrating renewable energy (RE) from 3 GW of offshore wind power near Bornholm, in conjunction with the international connection to Germany, which is set at 2 GW. The international connection to Germany is not part of this approval.  

In this context, the Danish Energy Agency considers that the design of the project, with a focus on future-proofing, also addresses the need for integrating additional renewable energy and international connections. The layout of the station on Bornholm, which allows for expansion with more offshore wind and additional international connections, is therefore considered to fall within the scope of the network expansion requirements.  

Additionally, the Danish Energy Agency assesses that the project will contribute to creating well-functioning competitive markets by establishing a transmission network between Zealand and a presumed future price zone, Bornholm.  

Based on Energinet's application and business case, it has been concluded that the project is needed. The assessment has taken into account the socioeconomic consequences of the project.  

In light of this, the Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities has a favorable view of the project's necessity and will finalize the application once the project has been presented to the Climate, Energy, and Utilities Committee.

686. ID: 521
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Reddit user
   Statement: Energy Islands are essentially expensive offshore transformers, collecting and conditioning electricity from offshore wind turbines. They produce no energy, but consume energy. The wind turbine electricity is converted from alternating to direct current at about 15% loss, is then sent via undersea cable to the nearby land. Between 10% and 30% of the raw wind power is converted by the wind turbine to electricity, then sent to the "Energy Island", converted again to direct current, sent to land where it is converted back to alternating current that is the same as the grid, another 15% loss, then forwarded to a customer. Denmark gets more electricity from burning down American forests as wood chips than from ALL her wind turbines and photovoltaics combined.

So far, globally, in the past decade more than 5 $TRILLION has been spent in the energy transition, and less than 5% of the total energy consumed is from wind and photovoltaics, not much of an accomplishment as we go bankrupt.

694. ID: 803
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Elisabetta M. Venco
   Statement: I, Elisabetta M. Venco from the University of Pavia, believe that Energy Communities are crucial for Europe's energy transition. These communities, where citizens actively participate in renewable energy projects, offer a more democratic and inclusive approach to energy systems. 

While renewable energy production and distributed consumption are distinct concepts, they can overlap, as seen in the "renewable islands" concept. Importantly, these communities are not just about renewable energy; they can involve various activities like energy efficiency, storage, and grid management. 

The EU's legal framework for Citizen Energy Communities (CEC) and Renewable Energy Communities (REC) has paved the way for their growth. These communities can significantly contribute to the energy market by: 

* Revitalizing local economies 
* Creating jobs 
* Increasing renewable energy investments 
* Optimizing the energy system 
* Decarbonizing Europe 

Citizen participation in these communities is driven by various factors, including economic, environmental, social, and political motivations. 
In the context of urban development, Energy Communities are vital for achieving sustainable energy solutions. They enhance citizen acceptance of renewable energy projects, attract private investment, and provide direct benefits to people, such as lower electricity bills. 

Europe's energy market is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving towards a distributed model with active citizen participation. I believe that citizens are the cornerstone of this energy transition, and their involvement is essential for its success.

710. ID: 6218
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We believe that it is prudent to maintain the option of overplanting for offshore wind on the Energy Islands. While overplanting does not increase the overall amount of electricity delivered to the grid beyond the production permit, it can offset transmission losses between turbines and the connection point. Additionally, overplanting can compensate for the occasional downtime of turbines due to maintenance or other factors, which can reduce the overall output of the wind farm. We want to clarify that overplanting will occur within the existing designated area for offshore wind farms, specifically within a maximum distance of 15 kilometers from the coast. To implement overplanting, wind farm developers will need to place turbines closer together than initially planned. If our environmental assessment indicates that a plan for 3.8 GW can be implemented without significant impacts, we would then allow wind farm developers to choose the economically optimal capacity within a range of 3.2 to 3.8 GW.

725. ID: 162
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Climate, Energy and Utilities Committee
   Statement: I have approved Energinet’s application for the "Energy Island Bornholm electrical infrastructure" project. The project involves establishing a 245 km direct current connection between Bornholm and Zealand, along with two 400 kV stations with converter facilities on Bornholm and Zealand. This infrastructure will connect Energy Island Bornholm to Denmark's electricity transmission grid.  

Following a political supplementary agreement on August 29, 2022, the Energy Island Bornholm project has been expanded from 2 GW to 3 GW. Additionally, a political agreement with Germany was reached on July 26, 2022, enabling Germany to connect to Energy Island Bornholm. Energinet has preliminarily assessed that this agreement will reduce the project’s budget due to cost-sharing with the German TSO, 50Hertz. As a result, Energinet’s construction budget has been reduced from 16.9 billion DKK to approximately 13.9 billion DKK, excluding risk costs. Similarly, annual operating costs have been reduced from 121 million DKK to 114 million DKK.  

Energinet’s application has been reviewed based on the submitted materials, including the technical solutions and assumptions outlined in the business case. The project must proceed in accordance with these specifications. Any significant changes to the project must be promptly reported to the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities for separate approval.

743. ID: 1563
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: Energy islands are essentially expensive offshore transformers that collect and condition electricity from offshore wind turbines. These islands do not produce energy but instead consume energy in the process. Electricity from wind turbines, which convert only 10% to 30% of raw wind power into electricity, is sent to the energy island and converted from alternating current to direct current, resulting in about a 15% energy loss. This electricity is then transmitted via undersea cables to land, where it is converted back to alternating current, causing another 15% loss, before being sent to customers. Denmark, for example, generates more electricity by burning American wood chips as biomass than from all its wind turbines and solar panels combined. Globally, over the past decade, more than $5 trillion has been spent on the energy transition, yet wind and solar power contribute less than 5% of total energy consumption—a small achievement while economies face financial strain.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   Actor: Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities
   Statement: We firmly believe that the development of offshore wind in the North Sea is a vital step toward electrifying Denmark and Europe. As we move toward a future where renewable energy sources must account for a much larger share of our energy consumption, we see this as a pivotal solution. By transitioning to green electricity, we can significantly reduce our dependence on fossil fuels, including Russian oil, coal, and gas.

The energy islands, which include artificial islands (such as Denmark’s energy island in the North Sea) and technical facilities on existing islands (like the energy island planned for Bornholm), represent a breakthrough in energy infrastructure. These islands will connect surrounding offshore wind farms to the electricity grids of multiple countries, enabling the distribution of green electricity directly to households and businesses across borders.

We are convinced that energy islands will enable the production of green electricity on an unprecedented scale. This innovation will help phase out fossil fuel-based energy production and pave the way for a more sustainable energy future. To ensure a reliable energy supply, even in a renewable-energy-driven system dependent on weather conditions, it is critical to fully harness the potential of the North Sea. Establishing a robust cross-border energy infrastructure will optimize our wind resources, and energy islands will play a central role in achieving this goal.

Moreover, energy islands will empower Europe to electrify large segments of society while making electricity consumption greener for households and businesses alike. These islands also have immense potential to serve as hubs for energy storage and for converting green electricity into sustainable fuels through Power-to-X technologies. This will provide solutions for heavy transportation sectors, such as aviation and shipping, further advancing our green transition.

We are committed to supporting these developments and ensuring that energy islands become a cornerstone of Europe’s sustainable energy future.

European renewable energy from the North Sea, including offshore wind and green hydrogen, contributing to both EU climate neutrality and energy security. To achieve this and to pave the way for the further expansion of offshore wind, we have decided to jointly develop The North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe, an offshore renewable energy

As Members of NSEC, we will build on the work already accomplished and will implement strategies to achieve our goals in close cooperation with the other regional countries and the European Commission. In doing so, we will strive for a balanced coexistence of economic and ecological needs. The North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe will consist of multiple connected offshore energy projects and hubs, offshore wind production at massive scale as well as electricity and green hydrogen interconnectors. We aim for a cost-efficient buildout of offshore wind that will harvest the potential of the North Sea in the most beneficial way for both the connected countries and the European Union overall.
Together, we have set ambitious combined targets for offshore wind of at least 65 GW by 2030. Based on the North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe, together we aim to more than double our total capacity of offshore wind to at least 150 GW by 2050, delivering more than half of capacity needed to reach EU climate neutrality according to the European Commission’s Strategy on Offshore Renewable Energy. This will contribute to large-scale onshore and offshore production of green hydrogen. We have set combined targets of about 20 GW production capacity already by 2030 and look to expand our production even further for 2050.

   Statement: The energy islands mark the beginning of a new era for the generation of energy from offshore wind, aimed at creating a green energy supply for Danish and foreign electricity grids. Operating as green power plants at sea, the islands are expected to play a major role in the phasing-out of fossil fuel energy sources in Denmark and Europe. 
After political agreement on the energy islands have been reached, the Danish Energy Agency plays a key role in leading the project that will transform the two energy islands from a vision to reality. The islands are pioneer projects that will necessitate the deployment of existing knowledge into an entirely new context. 
In the Baltic Sea, the electrotechnical equipment will be placed on the island of Bornholm, where electricity from offshore wind farms will be routed to electricity grids on Zealand and neighbouring countries. The offshore wind farms will be established approximately 15 km south-southwest of the coast and will be visible to the naked eye, but not dominate the horizon. The turbines off the coast of Bornholm will have an installed production capacity of up to 3,8 GW including overplanting. 
The location of the new windfarm is quite close to Bornholm and to Bornholm´s Airport at the South-Western corner of the island. Bornholm´s Airport is Denmark´s only state-owned airport administered by Trafikstyrelsen and operated by a local management team. The airport is as mentioned above located in the South Western corner of Bornholm with the coordinates 55°03′48″N 014°45′34″Ø close to Rønne town and to the sea in the western direction of the new windfarms. 
The airport has a 2002 m long and 45 m wide runway and service all kinds of aviation comprising: Scheduled passenger traffic mainly to Copenhagen, Charter traffic, Cargo traffic, General Aviation traffic (GA traffic), Search and Rescue traffic (SAR traffic), Military surveillance traffic. 
The airport is counted among the smaller airports in Denmark and had in 2021 180.000 arriving and departing passengers heavily influenced by the Corona pandemic. 
The location of Bornholm 1 and 2 will not interfere with the outer horizon for the instrument approach and landings with a 15 km distance between the windfarm and the airport. However, if the northern tip of the windfarm is moved closer to the airport to allow for more wind from the sea it may be necessary to move the upper rows of windmills to another location in the windfarm areas to avoid a conflict with the 15 km outer surface. The above-mentioned analysis of aviation related issues and scope of work will comprise civil traffic, military traffic, helicopter traffic and drone traffic.

774. ID: 6558
   Year: 2022
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: T. M. I. Riayatsyah
   Statement: The industrial revolution drastically transformed the world, leading to massive emissions from human activities. These actions have pushed the exploitation of Earth's natural resources to near irreversible limits. The consequences are evident in the extreme climate changes affecting many countries globally.  

One major contributor to climate change is energy generation, predominantly powered by fossil fuels such as coal and diesel. This process releases significant amounts of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide, which accelerates global warming. If fossil fuel consumption continues at its current pace, the planet faces catastrophic outcomes within a few decades.  

To address this issue, scientists and practitioners advocate for environmentally friendly energy alternatives. Renewable energy sources like hydropower, wind, and solar are increasingly promoted to power daily activities sustainably.  

Renewable energy has been extensively adopted in developed nations like the US, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Turkey, and the UK, where it is actively replacing harmful fossil fuels. However, in developing countries like Indonesia, renewable energy remains less popular due to the affordability of electricity from fossil fuels. For instance, Indonesia's energy mix in 2020 heavily favored fossil fuels, highlighting the need for policies and efforts to demonstrate the reliability of renewable energy as a viable alternative.  

Experiences from developed nations show that renewable energy is just as reliable as fossil fuel power plants. Additionally, new data reveals that renewable energy is now cheaper than fossil fuels in terms of levelized cost of energy (CoE), emphasizing its economic and environmental advantages.

   Statement: The large-scale export of electricity from the Danish Energy Island projects is actually an unintended consequence. After political consensus was reached for the island concept—and following numerous press releases about how Denmark would soon have all the energy it needs—someone discovered an EU directive that requires countries with major offshore wind projects to export 70% of the generated power. 

What you see here (in the referenced video and recent press releases) is an example of political spin. The result is that Denmark is financing the largest construction project in its history to export most of the electricity produced to neighboring countries at day rates.

This mandatory export and the confusing press messaging have several downsides. First, Power-to-X project leaders are left in a difficult position. More importantly, it makes it harder for Denmark to meet its decarbonization goals, which require access to large amounts of green electricity—a need the islands do not address. Additionally, funds that could have been invested in infrastructure, electrification, heat pumps, and other initiatives for decarbonization are now tied up in this export-focused project. This is especially unfortunate because Denmark is already a net importer of green electricity, meaning the country does not produce enough for its own needs.

On the positive side, it is beneficial that the EU has decided to strengthen the electricity grid in Europe and allocated significant funds for this purpose. For example, the COBRA cable to the Netherlands (operational since last autumn) and the Viking cable to the UK (underway but not yet completed) were financed through EU strategic funds, with more connections planned. Unfortunately, the same EU framework has also introduced mandatory export rules.

Denmark’s national transmission system operator, Energinet, provides a live overview of electricity flows into and out of the country via various links on its website for those interested in following this issue. We can only hope that neighboring countries suddenly develop a desire to build massive offshore wind farms that comply with the EU directive and are obligated to export to us—but realistically, we should not hold our breath.

Part of Denmark's energy strategy involves using excess wind power to produce green hydrogen and ammonia, essential for decarbonizing heavy industries like shipping (as seen with Maersk’s new ships) and aviation through e-fuels. To address the intermittency of wind energy, Denmark plans to convert excess wind power into an alternative energy medium, which can be stored and later discharged or burned when demand is high. The logic behind this strategy is to build overcapacity.

Denmark intends to develop the technologies and expertise necessary for the new green fuel economy, aiming to establish a thriving industry around it, similar to the success Denmark has had with offshore wind and energy technology exports. This long-term plan is a strategic bet for Denmark's future.

Building nuclear power plants in Denmark would not be politically feasible, as it would not gain support from the Danish populace. Additionally, Denmark lacks a domestic nuclear engineering labor force, especially when compared to the large pool of wind and sustainable energy engineers produced annually by Danish universities. These engineers are currently employed in the wind energy sector and are expected to work in the emerging Power-to-X industries.

825. ID: 5384
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: The concept of islands – historically seen as places of desire – is growing in relevance. Alongside natural islands, artificial ones are now being created. Denmark is currently planning the construction of an energy island in the North Sea, recognizing that the North Sea is the only genuinely large and reliable green power source in Europe. Is this a revolutionary concept? Not entirely. Similar visions for expanding Scharhörn into a significant energy hub in Hamburg arose during the 1960s oil crisis, known as the "Labskausdeal." Back then, the CEO of Salzgitter noted that no one in the steel industry could ignore Scharhörn.

For other Nordic nations, the idea proved too visionary and expensive, which led many energy-intensive companies from North Rhine-Westphalia to relocate to Belgium and the Netherlands. For Hamburg, this shift led to a focus on the Elbe metropolis and HafenCity with numerous river deepening projects, alongside a multi-billion-euro dredging operation funded by German taxpayers, yet lacking a genuine future outlook.

Now, Cuxhaven is positioning itself to capitalize on this opportunity for the northern countries with an island project that addresses the crucial challenges of today. We can eagerly anticipate the creation of the new, multifunctional "Watt'n Stoff Bundesinsel" (Federal Island).

831. ID: 962
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ministry of Energy, Utilities and Climate, Ministry for Economic Afairs and Climate Action
   Statement: We acknowledge the critical importance of energy security and combating climate change for the future of the European Union. We recognize that recent geopolitical events have highlighted the urgent need to replace fossil fuels, especially Russian oil, coal, and gas, with European renewable energy from the North Sea, including offshore wind electricity and green hydrogen, to support both EU climate neutrality and energy security. 

We further acknowledge the cooperation established between Denmark, Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands in the “Esbjerg Declaration” of May 18th, 2022, which envisions the North Sea as a Green Power Plant of Europe. In our view, offshore renewable energy hubs and a meshed offshore grid are essential for generating, connecting, converting, and transporting offshore wind energy in the North Sea. 

We note Germany’s plans to establish offshore renewable energy clusters with a 10 GW capacity in the North Sea by the mid-2030s and Denmark’s plans to create a Danish Energy Island with up to 10 GW capacity by 2040. Additionally, we recall the EU Marine Strategy Directive and our joint commitment to achieving good environmental status for all European seas, including the North Sea.

We have agreed on the necessity of this Joint Declaration of Intent (JDoI) to focus on cooperation for connecting Germany’s planned offshore renewable energy hubs with Denmark’s Energy Island. Our primary objective is to facilitate mutual benefits by improving energy security, increasing socio-economic welfare, diversifying energy sources, meeting EU and national renewable energy targets, and integrating wind power with hydrogen and Power-to-X technologies.

To achieve this, we propose the establishment of a Joint Working Group led by energy ministries, supported by energy authorities and Transmission System Operators (TSOs). This group will develop a pre-feasibility study analyzing technical, environmental, and economic aspects and deliver a joint recommendation by the first half of 2024. This recommendation will guide the next steps toward realizing the project, aiming for implementation by the mid-2030s.

We emphasize that this JDoI creates no binding obligations under international law and imposes no financial commitments unless mutually agreed. Cooperation costs are borne by the respective Participant. Any amendments to this JDoI require joint written consent, and any misunderstandings will be resolved collaboratively in good faith and mutual trust. 

This JDoI takes effect upon signature and may be terminated with three months' written notice. Termination does not affect ongoing activities unless otherwise decided.

Signed on April 24th, 2023, in Ostende.

That fuel must be in demand, and the vehicles and machinery powered by it must be ready—either specifically designed for the purpose or modified so their engines can run on sustainable fuels.

If this development does not happen quickly enough, there will be too much electricity for the grid. This would require further reinforcement of the grid, which is already expensive. According to a report by the consultancy Rambøll from March 7 this year (2023), the grid expansion will cost 110 billion kroner, which is 30 billion more than estimated in 2020. Such a significant expansion also takes time, and it is doubtful whether it can be completed in time.

Meanwhile, the large amounts of surplus electricity from the energy island during periods of high wind would either go to waste or be sold at extremely low prices. For instance, one cannot simply rely on exporting to Germany, which is also undergoing a significant expansion of offshore wind farms.

838. ID: 3551

   Cluster: (None)

   Statement: The energy island is designed to connect to the grid via a multiterminal high-voltage direct current (MTHVDC) system—a concept still untested on the scale required for onshore grids. Existing MTHVDC systems have limitations unsuitable for energy islands, highlighting the need for research, development, and standardization efforts from suppliers and operators.

Rushing the project risks dependency on a single supplier, complicating future tenders and integration of new technologies. A failure in the MTHVDC system would harm project economics and reduce green energy availability.

Historically, grid development has been incremental, enabling adaptation. Implementing a large-scale system all at once risks durability issues, as untested replacements and interactions between old and new equipment may create challenges.

The project consists of three main components:
1. Offshore wind farms south and west of Bornholm
2. A cable connection to Germany, being established by our German colleagues at 50Hertz Transmission GmbH
3. Energinet's facilities, which include two converter stations (one on Bornholm and one on Zealand) and a 1.2 GW DC connection between them

The Øbisserne team has assisted the Danish Energy Agency in preparing the environmental impact assessment that accompanies the Energy Island Bornholm plan, both for marine and land-based aspects. This assessment outlines the environmental consequences of a fully developed Energy Island Bornholm at a general level, helping us understand how to best consider environmental factors during construction.

All interested parties can access the consultation materials and submit responses until December 1st through the Danish Energy Agency's website.

859. ID: 1000
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Reddit user
   Statement: One negative I am aware of is that HVDC does not allow for the transmission of VAR power, meaning there’s no voltage support at the reception end. While using a 2-conductor line significantly reduces material costs compared to a 3-conductor line, the equipment at each end for rectification and inversion is much more expensive and results in significant efficiency losses. The power lost during conversion is not negligible, and the equipment generates heat, making it temperature-sensitive, which limits its availability during peak ambient heat conditions—typically when demand is highest. This is also when voltage support is most needed, which further compounds the issue.

869. ID: 3593

   Statement: Denmark’s specialty is wind energy. They made the political decision 50 years ago to abandon nuclear power, and it has worked well for them.

Part of this strategy involves using excess wind power to produce green hydrogen and ammonia, which is crucial for the energy transition to decarbonize heavy industries like shipping (as seen with Maersk’s new ships) and aviation through e-fuels. The intermittency of wind can be addressed by converting excess power into an alternative energy medium, which can then be stored or burned when supply exceeds demand. The logic here is to build overcapacity.

Denmark will develop the necessary technologies and expertise in the green fuel economy, creating a new industry, much like they have done with offshore wind and other energy technology exports. This is a long-term plan, and it’s a strategy they are fully committed to.

Building nuclear power in Denmark would never gain political support from the population, so it’s a moot point. Additionally, there is no domestic labor pool for nuclear engineering. In contrast, Denmark produces hundreds of wind and sustainable energy engineers from universities every year, who already contribute to the current wind industry and the future power-to-X sectors.

893. ID: 869
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Journalist
   Statement: While researchers may calculate that it is theoretically possible to base energy supply on wind and solar power, I believe it is not desirable for several reasons.

First, there will inevitably be numerous challenges in translating theory into practice, leading to delays in the energy transition and prolonged dependence on fossil fuels.

Second, Power-to-X technology is not yet mature, and there are no facilities currently capable of delivering the scale of energy needed to power an entire country. Politicians are gambling on the rapid development of this technology, but there is no guarantee it will be ready when needed. Additionally, storing and transporting large quantities of energy for periods with no wind or solar power—such as calm, foggy weeks in January—presents significant logistical challenges.

The North Sea Energy Island is projected to cost 210 billion kroner, providing an installed capacity of 3 GW of wind turbines, with an actual average output of 1.5 GW due to a capacity factor of 50%. This must cover electricity consumption, Power-to-X needs, and electrified district heating. The Energy Island is not expected to be operational until 2033. By comparison, Poland has agreed to purchase six APR 1400 nuclear reactors from South Korea’s Kepco for 202 billion kroner, providing 8.4 GW installed capacity and 7.98 GW effective output due to a 95% capacity factor. The first reactor is expected to deliver electricity to the Polish grid by 2030. Nuclear power can also provide district heating, reducing the need for additional electricity. Given Denmark’s energy needs of 4–5 GW, the Polish model would offer surplus capacity for exports, synthetic fuels, or cost savings by building fewer reactors.

A wind- and solar-powered grid would require substantial technological solutions, such as using electric vehicle batteries to buffer fluctuations. A stable supply from nuclear power would eliminate the need for these costly and unnecessary innovations, reduce wear on expensive batteries, and avoid changing consumption habits—arguably one of the most challenging tasks.

It has been documented that wind power requires more than twice the resources (concrete, steel, copper, etc.) to deliver the same amount of energy as nuclear power.

Denmark currently imports hydropower from Norway during shortages, but Norway has faced decreasing rainfall in recent years, limiting its ability to export electricity. Norwegian energy officials have also stated that Norway neither can nor wishes to serve as a buffer for Northern Europe. Even Norway is debating nuclear power due to doubts about the long-term reliability of hydropower.

In summary, while it might be theoretically possible to rely on wind and solar power, I do not believe there is sufficient time to develop, build, and implement the necessary solutions or to change consumption habits. This approach risks prolonging our reliance on fossil fuels such as coal or deforestation-based biomass.

902. ID: 3715
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: LinkedIn user
   Statement: The Danish energy island will not be the first in the North Sea, which could put economic pressure on the project, but there will still be market space for electricity production. Belgium and Germany are already well underway with establishing energy islands in the North Sea, and the Netherlands and the United Kingdom are following closely behind. They have all seen the idea and are in the process of planning and procuring materials.

Overall, our neighboring countries in the North Sea are expected to be ready to send 11.3 GW of electricity from offshore wind turbines to the European electricity market within the same timeframe as Denmark or even faster. Meanwhile, the start date for the Danish energy island has been pushed from 2030 to 2033, and Danish actors are still waiting for tender materials from the Danish Energy Agency. However, the fact that other countries have progressed further in their efforts to establish their energy islands does not necessarily have to be a major problem for Denmark, says Lena Kitzing, an associate professor and head of the Society, Market, and Policy research group at the DTU Wind Energy and Energy Systems Department.

Last year, she and her colleagues published an article in the journal Energies, in which they quantified the socioeconomic value of offshore networks and identified their main drivers using a model of how Europe's energy system will develop up to 2050 – including offshore wind.

Using the model, the researchers concluded that in terms of decarbonizing the future energy system, it would be socioeconomically optimal to establish 214 GW of interconnected energy islands in the North Sea – equivalent to at least eight to nine islands, each in the range of 20 GW or more. In the analysis, the researchers did not consider islands larger than 24 GW. Most will likely be slightly smaller – especially at the beginning of development.

"Our calculations show that there is a need for more energy islands in the North Sea – maybe around eight when we look towards 2050. So, it is not the case that one country can hinder another country's plans to build an energy island by rushing to build first. All North Sea countries will likely get energy islands in the future," says Lena Kitzing.

It was never expected that the Danish island would be the only one, but the question is whether it is a problem that it now will not even come in second, but more likely last?

"Those who exploit the resource first get the greatest economic advantage. Therefore, each new energy island will shift the price picture for electricity from offshore wind turbines in the North Sea in general," says Carsten Chachah, senior chief consultant at Greenpower Denmark. However, the consulting firm Ea Energy Analysis is pushing to get the planning started:

"We know that an energy island is a good idea, there have been enough analyses to establish that. In 50 years, we may conclude that it was not the best layout and that there may have been solutions that were a bit cheaper. But right now, I believe that speed is more important than perfection," says partner Hans Henrik Lindboe.

910. ID: 4578
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: We acknowledges that some components in high-voltage systems may contain potent greenhouse gases, such as SF6 (sulfur hexafluoride), commonly used in high-voltage components over 100 kV and as an insulating medium in Gas Insulated Switchgear (GIS). SF6 is a powerful greenhouse gas, 25,200 times more potent than CO₂ and with an atmospheric lifespan of 3,200 years. Emissions occur during filling, leaks, and similar processes.

The implementation of the Energy Island Bornholm program will enable the construction of high-voltage systems on Bornholm and Zealand, which may lead to unintended emissions of SF6 during operation. However, the anticipated emissions are assessed as having no significant climate impact due to their limited contribution relative to municipal and national carbon inventories. Over time, SF6 will be gradually replaced with alternatives that have a lower climate footprint. If future high-voltage systems are built using SF6 and the estimated emissions occur, the negative effects can be mitigated by utilizing agricultural land. Overall, the impact on the climate is expected to be minimal, and the plan's realization may result in a small net positive effect.

911. ID: 4579
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: To implement the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm, cables may need to be installed through three Natura 2000 areas on land: N148 Køge Å, N149 Tryggevælde Å, and N187 Kystskrænter ved Arnager Bugt. A significance assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential impacts on these areas.

All cable installations within Natura 2000 areas will use guided horizontal drilling. The only potential impact identified is the risk of unintended drilling mud leaks. The significance assessment concludes that a significant impact on the designation basis of Natura 2000 area N187 can be ruled out because the habitat types within the area are not vulnerable to such leaks. Similarly, most habitat types and species in areas N148 and N149 are not vulnerable, but potential impacts on nutrient-rich lake habitats in N148 and lagoon habitats in N149 cannot be ruled out. Consequently, an impact assessment was conducted for these two habitat types.

Since the identified vulnerable habitats are small and located on the edges of the plan area, potential damage can be avoided by conducting drilling outside these sensitive habitats. The conclusion of the impact assessment is that the realization of the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm, either individually or in combination with other projects, will not risk harming the habitat types in the Natura 2000 designation basis. This is contingent on implementing all relevant mitigation measures in future projects. Based on this, the integrity of the Natura 2000 areas will not be compromised by the implementation of the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm on land.

912. ID: 4580

   Statement: We emphasize that species listed under Annex IV of the EU Habitats Directive are subject to strict protection throughout the EU. These Annex IV species must not be disturbed, killed, or have their breeding and resting habitats damaged. Some of these species are common in Denmark, while others are rarer. Within the planning areas for the Energy Island projects and a 2 km buffer zone surrounding them, surveys have identified the presence of Annex IV species. Certain species, such as amphibians, are known to migrate between breeding ponds and resting areas.

The environmental assessment for the Plan for the Energy Island project at Bornholm includes evaluations of both potential temporary and permanent impacts, including physical interventions. These potential impacts are expected to arise from the temporary or permanent use of land and activities associated with the construction of high-voltage installations, as well as the burial and horizontal directional drilling of cables.

The surveys have recorded the following Annex IV species on Zealand: great crested newt, agile frog, common frog, viviparous lizard, and green hawker dragonfly, along with several bat species. On Bornholm, the species recorded include the great diving beetle, viviparous lizard, tree frog, natterjack toad, and common frog.

919. ID: 4589
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Technical University of Denmark
   Statement: Fortunately, the potential for wind power in the open sea is vast. However, the technical concept used for wind farms near the coast will not work in the open sea. For the near-shore parks we know today, the electricity is produced as alternating current (AC), which is transmitted directly through cables to the grid on land. The distance to parks in open water means that the electricity must be converted to direct current (DC) in order to be sent to land. The equipment responsible for converting the electricity – so-called converters – is so large that a physical structure is needed close to the production site. In other words, without energy islands, it will not be possible to expand offshore wind power on the scale that has been planned.

An added benefit is that there may be opportunities to place other types of production on the islands. This could include the production of hydrogen or green fuels for aviation, industry, heavy traffic, and shipping. This is also known as Power-to-X. The production of such fuels is a necessary condition for achieving the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global average temperature changes to no more than just under two degrees, or preferably no more than 1.5 degrees.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is approximately five times the cost of the Great Belt Bridge. No one in the world has built anything in renewable energy on this physical and economic scale. An energy island is not a product that can be taken off the shelf. Many solutions are not ready yet. Therefore, there is a need for fundamentally new solutions for managing the electricity system on an energy island. Even for the elements that are well-known – such as the offshore wind turbines themselves – there is a high likelihood of achieving significant advantages by tailoring them specifically to integrate into an energy island.

926. ID: 4574
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The realization of the Energy Island Bornholm plan has the potential to affect soil conditions due to the possibility of municipalities altering land use within the planned areas. These potential effects on soil include land appropriation, soil compaction, contamination, and changes to groundwater levels. Experience from similar projects shows that soil impact is most significant during the establishment of high-voltage installations, while the impacts of laying land cables are temporary and less severe.

On both Bornholm and Zealand, there are significant areas with freshwater formations within the planning zones for high-voltage installations. These areas will be further investigated to identify potential deep peat and organic soil zones as part of specific construction considerations. It is assessed that the construction enabled by the plan can proceed without significant impacts.

There are no extensive areas with identified soil contamination within the planned zones for land cables and high-voltage installations. The construction enabled by the plan is considered feasible without a risk of increased contamination spread, including to groundwater, provided any contaminated soil is managed according to current legislation. The risk of increased soil contamination is deemed low, as contaminated sites can be avoided, and any affected soil will be handled according to established guidelines. Overall, it is assessed that there will be no significant impact on soil from the realization of the plan.

On Zealand, several parts of the planned zones for land cables and the landing of submarine cables overlap with lowland areas identified in municipal plans. Guided drilling is used to install cables under lowland areas, which minimizes significant impacts. However, establishing high-voltage installations and other fixed facilities, such as joint bays, on lowland areas may require additional drainage, potentially leading to ochre leakage. Despite this, it is possible to place joint bays outside designated lowland areas to avoid such impacts. High-voltage installations can also be established outside lowland areas on both Zealand and Bornholm. Consequently, the impact on lowland areas is assessed as negligible, and the overall effect is not considered significant.

I can now finally give the market the green light for the expansion of potentially 14 GW of offshore wind or more – and for the first time, I and the state will become co-owners of most of them, thereby gaining a share of the actual revenues from offshore wind. I am introducing new sustainability requirements and establishing a Marine Nature Fund, so nature is also considered. The next chapter must now be written in collaboration with market actors, as they are the ones who must take the lead,” says Climate, Energy, and Utilities Minister Lars Aagaard.

“I have entered into a broad agreement that sets the framework for a historically large expansion of green electricity. Denmark’s maritime areas will become a driving force in the green transition – not just in Denmark, but across Europe. The agreement will also strengthen energy security and support Danish strengths and jobs. At the same time, it will contribute to making Europe more independent of, for example, Russian gas. Finally, the agreement ensures that society as a whole benefits from the returns on Denmark’s wind resources,” says Acting Minister for Economic Affairs Stephanie Lose.

“This is, in every way, a historic day. With this agreement, I am utilizing and developing my strengths in offshore wind on a historic scale. This must happen in cooperation between the state and the business sector. And it will be very concrete: The agreement parties agree that the state should be a co-owner of the individual offshore wind farms. To ensure that the Danish society gets a fair share of future revenues when our shared maritime resource is used for offshore wind. Co-ownership is a stamp of confidence for developers that the government wants to invest in the green transition – together with them and for the benefit of society as a whole,” says Minister for Business Morten Bødskov.

959. ID: 4831
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Job creation and innovation
   Actor: Claus M. Andersen
   Statement: This might be the most groundbreaking project we’ve landed in the 15 years we’ve hosted research and demonstration projects.

The Combined Heat and Power Plant on Skansevej in Rønne will soon house the Second Life for Powerplants project.

A number of European pioneers in energy technology have teamed up to solve one of the biggest challenges in sustainable transition: capturing and storing energy from solar and wind power, ensuring electricity and heat are available even on cloudy, windless days. The project budget is DKK 100 million, with EU support amounting to DKK 60 million.

The idea behind Second Life for Powerplants is to repurpose existing power plant technology while building on employees' skills. This means reusing the steam turbine, generator, control systems, and connections to the electricity grid and district heating network. The power plant will be equipped with three new storage technologies: a salt storage system, used electric vehicle batteries, and a high-tech flywheel battery. At the core of the concept is an advanced control software designed to ensure the availability of electricity and heat – even on overcast days with no wind.

"We will gain invaluable knowledge about how to handle and store solar and wind energy in the future – and how to effectively ensure balance in the electricity system. We will obtain solid insights into what it takes to fully utilize solar and wind power without significantly increasing costs for Bornholm’s residents. We will also get clear indications of the investments required to finally say goodbye to oil and phase out wood chips," I explained.

I also pointed out that the experiences gained from the project on Bornholm can be easily replicated elsewhere, making it much easier, cheaper, and faster to convert, for instance, a Polish coal power plant into a flexible energy storage facility for solar and wind power.

"The fact that we could land such a project on Bornholm might suggest that we should consider raising our expectations about the additional activity the Bornholm Energy Island will generate for the island," I concluded.
