983. ID: 7081
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Beirut International
   Statement: Offshore wind energy generation is more efficient than on land, to harness it you’d have to follow the wind. Ocean water currents offer a much higher energy density, at a stable rate, the technology is progressing, to harness you’d have to follow the currents. 
To make Hydrogen Green, sea water reverse osmosis and electrolysis equipment have to be close to an energy source, from here the idea of Energy Islands begins. 

Energy Islands should be near the winds, waves and currents. The Baltic Sea average depth is 50 m, the North Sea 90 m, the Mediterranean Sea 1,500 m, the Atlantic Ocean 3,600 m.

Energy Islands should be accessible all year long. Offshore rigs personnel have to go through extensive safety training to be allowed to make the trip by Helicopter or by Offshore Support Vessels, both ways are expensive and at high risk.
Energy Islands should cater for additional space when an Wind Farm expands; and permit ergonomic maintenance and replacement of equipment without the use of heavy lift Floating Marine Cranes and Floating Docks.

Energy Islands service and operations teams may range from dozens to hundreds. This team require fresh water supply, food supply, cold service water, hot service water, wastewater disposal, solid waste disposal and regular rotation.  Offshore supply and retrieval trips made by Offshore Supply Vessels is dangerous and expensive in high seas.

Supposing a nation wishes to build an Energy Island by backfilling into the sea within its economic water zone; the currents within this sea would have to be studied not to alter direction and affect neighboring nations, the sediments from the backfilling process would be carried to undesirable locations within the nation shoreline, or to neighboring shoreline, affecting marine fauna and flora. A thorough Environmental Impact Assessment should be endorsed by all nation stakeholders.
Assuming an EIA is approved, lets look at the backfilling process on a sandy bed at 50 m seawater depth. If the surface footprint of the island is to be 500m x 500m, the scour protection measures, whatever the method used, would have a footprint of around 600m x 600m at sea bed level. The offshore contracting operations would have to be carried out within the yearly calm season, if the entire operation, or the milestone target construction is not achieved within the first season, the sea would destroy and remove most of it before the next season.
 After completion, if a structural failure occurs, under rough sea conditions, repairs would have to wait till the calm season, at the risk of further uncontrollable damage.
Once such Energy Island is completed, installing equipment on top would follow any port procedures; if certain components need to be replaced, they would have to be lifted and transported onto a vessel.
While this enormous offshore marine contracting job maybe concluded at 50m depth, will let the reader imagine the 90m or 1,500m sea depth scenario feasibility.

A Floating Island is fabricated in a shipyard, launched to sea, tugged to the desired location, and anchored. The process is carried in a controlled environment, irrespective of sea state and sea depth.
While many Floating Island solutions are marketed, and most developers submitted their design to the UN Habitat in 2018 in a New York meeting, none of their literature is conclusive, most of it is at conceptual level. 
The only solution that passed Two Marine Societies design approval by Bureau Veritas  in 2005 and International Naval Survey Bureau in 2009, and a thorough Marine Society design, engineering, procurement and fabrication survey by INSB from 2009 till 2015 is the one made by Dr. Abdullah Daou, the founder of Beirut International Marine Industry and Commerce. 
Beirut International’s Floating Island first prototype was made in 1997, at a scale of 1:10 measuring 4m x 4m, was extensively tested in a make shift water basin, with better than expected stability results under high simulated waves condition.

In 2009 the fabrication of the first Floating Island made by Beirut International started in Lebanon. The substructure base 48m wide, by 76m long, 9m deep and weighing around 4,000 tons was being assembled in Tripoli Shipyard, while structural components where being fabricated in three other workshops in Lebanon by a team of 431 local technicians and engineers. 
While the fate of this structure was unfortunate, Ninety-Eight Million US Dollars were invested in the research, development and fabrication; a 70% completion rate was achieved, almost all drawings approved and stamped by INSB meeting SOLAS and other marine regulations. 
The learning curve is priceless. The technology is ready, far ahead of any contender. True, a full-scale prototype is yet to be made again and tested.


There is seven pros for building the energy islands.
A Floating Energy Island is modular, making it scalable to meet any Offshore Wind Farm expansion. If maintenance is requires, a module can be detached, tugged to a shipyard then re-connected.
The substructure of a Floating Energy Island is transparent to the sea, making it an artificial coral reef for marine life, and simultaneously providing anchoring points to install Water Current Energy makers. 
The waves are absorbed and damped by the Floating Energy Island, creating a calm water area at the rear port for Vessel to approach and dock at ease, allowing for safe and friendly access. 
Being a generator of Hydrogen, and having a large underwater space, it is an ideal location to develop sustainable fisheries, creating an additional export income.
Solid waste composting and wastewater treatment available technologies can make some agriculture a sustainable alternative to waste disposal.
The Hydrogen process being noiseless, and clean; a Yacht Club can be safe haven for yachts sailing across seas and oceans.

However the cons of building the islands are yet to be tested by our firm.

The Hydrogen Environment is relatively new. 
Stakeholders include: Shipping Companies, Energy Companies, Ports Logistics, Telecommunication, Reverse Osmosis Water Makers, Electroliser Makers, Wind Turbine makers, Wave Energy Makers, Current Energy Makers, Shipyards, Marine Offshore Contractors, Hydrogen Storage Solution Makers, Inverters, Controls, Aquaponics, Wastewater Treatment, Solid Waste Treatment… 
While some stakeholders are more advanced then the other, some at prototyping stage, other at maturity; a Floating Energy Island success needs their close collaboration. A fresh firm in the Legal field is trying to advise stakeholders to join efforts and Joint Venture to make such infrastructure and energy concepts a needed reality to meet a Marine Decarbonization.

This formal requirement was finalized during Thursday’s session, moving us closer to realizing this significant project for Nexø Havn.

1001. ID: 5275
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: German collaboration
   Actor: Energinet
   Statement: Denmark and Germany have signed a milestone agreement for Energy Island Bornholm, with Germany now investing in the infrastructure to transport electricity from Energy Island Bornholm to the German market via an undersea power cable running from Bornholm's high-voltage facility to Germany.

Energinet and German transmission operator 50Hertz will each cover half of the infrastructure costs for the project and equally share the renewable energy portions generated by the project. The two operators will also equally distribute the congestion income from the power connections between the countries.

Beyond financial commitments, Germany is taking on partial responsibility for Energy Island Bornholm. Energinet and 50Hertz are not only initiating pioneering technical work - negotiations between the two companies and governments have also clarified ownership structures and distribution of energy quantities that can contribute to both countries' renewable energy goals.

This formalization of German involvement in Energy Island Bornholm, which was initially arranged in August 2022, was completed when Danish Climate Minister Lars Aagaard and German Economy Minister Robert Habeck signed the agreement at the European energy ministers' meeting in Luxembourg. This agreement represents a crucial cornerstone for Energy Island Bornholm.

1003. ID: 361
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: WindEurope
   Statement: The North Sea has the potential to host more than 200 offshore wind farms, each with a capacity of 1 GW, due to its strong winds and shallow waters. However, achieving this requires building wind farms far from the coast, which significantly increases the cost of electrical infrastructure. Alternating current does not transmit efficiently over long distances, necessitating the use of more expensive direct current substations and cabling.

Building an energy island transforms this scenario. An energy island allows for the pooling of electrical infrastructure—such as transformers and cables—connecting the wind farms to the mainland, thereby reducing the required investment. Additionally, an energy island enables the delivery of electricity to multiple countries instead of a single national grid. This makes it easier to sell electricity at the best price when wind farms are operating at full capacity, without risking instability in any single grid.

1030. ID: 7009
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Jacob Østergaard
   Statement: Producing hydrogen at a scale of 1 GW requires approximately 1.8 million cubic meters of water annually. This water must be ultrapure, necessitating extensive treatment before seawater can be used. Additionally, high-quality cooling water is required due to the significant generation of waste heat during hydrogen production. A major technical challenge involves designing pipelines suitable for both hydrogen transport and corrosive seawater environments.

Current state-of-the-art seawater desalination technologies, such as reverse osmosis, are complex, require high maintenance, and consume significant amounts of energy. However, thermal integration of electrolyzers with seawater desalination processes could create a more dynamic and efficient system capable of handling the fluctuating water demands for future offshore hydrogen production.

An alternative approach would be developing electrolysis technologies capable of tolerating salt or seawater directly. However, a key challenge is that hydrogen interacts with many metals, expanding their lattice structure and compromising mechanical integrity under high pressure.

There is a critical need for further research in two areas: the development of reliable, efficient, and compact seawater desalination systems, and the creation of advanced materials that are both corrosion-resistant and capable of maintaining structural integrity under high hydrogen pressures.

The land use in areas where cables are being laid will primarily be affected during the construction phase, as these areas will be restored to their original state after the cables are buried. In the operational phase, the areas where cables are laid will be subject to a servitude related to planting and similar activities, but otherwise, these areas can be used as before.

Recreational activities such as walking on paths and beaches, sports activities, and hunting may be temporarily impacted during the construction phase, with potential noise disturbances and short-term rerouting or closures of paths and roads. Work sites will be fenced off for safety reasons, and the public will not have access to these areas.

1048. ID: 4348
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Financial viability and (un)profitability
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: The North Sea energy island project has encountered significant financial challenges. The project, which was supposed to serve as a hub for collecting and distributing electricity from offshore wind turbines located 80–100 kilometers off the west coast of Jutland, is currently estimated to cost the state over 50 billion kroner. This far exceeds the acceptable level of financial viability required by the political agreements that underpin the project.

Given these economic obstacles, the Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities will spend the next six months exploring alternative designs to make the project less complex and more affordable. The current model, developed since 2020, has proven to be too costly and risky. To address these issues, I, Lars Aagaard, Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities, am considering lessons from other North Sea countries. These countries have opted for simpler steel structure platforms to reduce costs. Another potential cost-saving measure involves accelerating the construction of some offshore wind turbines, which would generate power for the energy island sooner.

Despite the delays, the government remains committed to the ambition of realizing the North Sea energy island. However, adjustments must be made to ensure the project is economically viable. It is essential to move quickly, as the energy island needs to be operational shortly after 2030 to meet energy goals. We will engage in discussions with businesses, investors, and the Danish Parliament to find viable solutions and proceed responsibly without unnecessary haste.

The challenges are significant, but they reflect the scale and innovation required for a project of this nature, which has never been attempted before.

1059. ID: 2593

   Statement: I highlight a coordination problem between the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy, using Denmark's planned North Sea energy island as an example. The long gap between the project's announcement and its start in 2033 could lead to a 'Green Paradox,' where emissions actually increase in the EU ETS due to the way the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) functions. My study shows that the leakage rate in 2050 could be as high as 145%, and I suggest potential solutions to improve the climate benefits of large-scale projects like this. These include revising the EU ETS or utilizing Power-to-X technologies, though these won't fully resolve the coordination failure. One option is removing the MSR or adjusting the emission cap to give politicians more control over long-term emissions, but this could increase leakage effects and price volatility. In conclusion, there is no easy solution to this problem.

1074. ID: 2691
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: The Climate, Energy, and Utilities Committee has asked me, in a letter dated June 1, 2023, to answer the following question, which was requested by Steffen W. Frølund (LA). The question concerns the consequences of applying the same tariff model, expected to be used for Energiø Bornholm, to all renewable energy (RE) electricity producers connected at the transmission level.

I must first note that according to the market directive, it is the collective electricity supply companies that develop tariff methods, and the Energy Regulatory Authority (Forsyningstilsynet) that approves them. This means that the Minister or the Parliament has very limited ability to dictate tariff designs.

The tariff pricing methods must, among other things, adhere to the principle of cost-reflectiveness, meaning they must reflect the costs incurred by the various categories of network users. In connection with this, Energinet has informed me that the general tariff model for producer payments specifically excludes electricity production connected to energy islands. This is because the standardized connection fee now applied for electricity production cannot, in a cost-reflective manner, accommodate the payment required for connection to energy islands. The transmission network at and near energy islands is of a special nature, as it includes both trade connections to foreign countries and specialized installations for connecting offshore wind, which also involves significantly higher investment costs compared to, for example, the connection of a typical offshore wind farm or larger solar park.

As a result, Energinet is currently developing a tariff financing model for Energinet’s costs related to energy islands. This model was sent for public consultation on May 3, 2023, with a response deadline of June 6, 2023. The draft tariff model proposes that the offshore wind connected to an energy island will be tariffed according to the costs it incurs. This draft includes, among other things, that electricity producers and consumers will share the financing of parts of Energinet’s costs using a distribution key specially developed for financing Energinet’s costs related to energy islands in order to allocate these costs in a cost-reflective manner.

Such a distribution key cannot be applied to tariffing other RE electricity producers, as they do not contribute to the financing of trade connections as part of their connection to the grid. This is because other RE electricity producers are not directly dependent on specific trade connections in their grid connection and the sale of their production, like the offshore wind connected at Energiø Bornholm.

1103. ID: 2835
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Jakob Nørmark
   Statement: The introduction of a separate electricity price zone for Bornholm tied to the Energy Island will likely result in slightly cheaper electricity for Bornholm residents. However, this price difference is expected to be minimal. The new zone will only take effect if Bornholm’s grid is connected directly to the Energy Island's high-voltage infrastructure, enabling local access to offshore wind energy.  

If no such connection is established due to complexity or cost, Bornholm will remain part of the existing eastern Denmark (DK2) price zone, and an offshore price zone will instead cover only the wind farms and island infrastructure. In this scenario, Bornholm would continue to rely solely on its cable connection to Sweden.  

The purpose of the new price zone is to make the limitations of the transmission capacity between Bornholm, Zealand, and Germany visible to the market. Without this, the market could mistakenly assume that unlimited energy transfers are possible, leading to imbalances and costly corrective measures for Energinet, and by extension, the Danish public.  

The expected price benefit arises from market mechanisms where Bornholm’s spot price will align with the lowest neighboring price—either Zealand’s or Germany’s—depending on capacity availability. However, the price differences between these regions are usually minor. Under normal circumstances, the spot price only constitutes about 23% of the total consumer electricity bill, with taxes and tariffs making up the majority. Therefore, a lower wholesale price will only marginally impact overall consumer costs.  

Certain conditions, such as maintenance or cable damage, could cause energy production to exceed cable capacity, leading to temporarily lower prices on Bornholm. Conversely, if offshore wind production is low and cables are fully utilized, Bornholm’s price could match the higher German rates.  

Ultimately, the effect of a new price zone will depend on the evolving structure of the Energy Island project, such as additional wind capacity or the construction of large electricity-consuming facilities like power-to-X plants, which could either decrease or increase local electricity prices accordingly.

1113. ID: 5711
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: ELECTA research group
   Statement: We conducted a preliminary assessment of the concept for a Mediterranean energy island in Sardinia, linking Italy, France, and Spain with HVDC interconnections. Our initial findings indicate significant benefits for Europe, including reduced operational costs and lower CO2 emissions for the DE and GA scenarios of ENTSO-E’s TYNDP. Using a European nodal model, we observed even greater benefits in terms of operational costs and CO2 emissions, as the investment also alleviates internal grid congestion.

We performed a preliminary economic assessment of the investment costs for the entire energy island. The estimated costs range from 5.98 billion to 7.04 billion euros for 1 GW HVDC links and from 11.96 billion to 19.53 billion euros for 2 GW HVDC links, which are comparable to current projects. However, a case-specific investigation is necessary for more accurate figures.

Future work will include detailed nodal simulations for Sardinia’s and Corsica’s grids, additional scenarios, more planning years, and the option to run OPFs for selected market zones. We will also develop more risk-aware power flow control simulations to account for potential HVDC link faults. Planned refinements include Security-constrained Optimal Power Flow, unbalanced operation of bipolar HVDC links, and topological actions for meshed AC/DC grids.

1132. ID: 1483
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Siemens Energy
   Statement: In this article, we wish to bring awareness and create some thoughtful conversations surrounding emerging technological philosophies. Specifically, Sector coupling and Power-to-X.

Sector coupling and Power-to-X are two related concepts that have emerged, globally, as key strategies in the transition towards a more sustainable and climate-neutral energy system.

At the forefront of this technological and philosophical advancement is Siemens Energy 

Sector coupling refers to the integration of different energy sectors, such as electricity, heating, cooling, and transportation, in a way that maximizes the efficient use of renewable energy sources. The goal is to create a more flexible, efficient, and resilient energy system that can better accommodate the fluctuations in renewable energy supply.

Power-to-X, on the other hand, refers to the conversion of renewable electricity into other forms of energy, such as hydrogen, synthetic fuels, or chemicals. These energy carriers can be used to decarbonize other sectors, such as transportation, heating, or industry, that are difficult to electrify directly.

Together, sector coupling and Power-to-X can help to create a circular economy of energy, where renewable energy sources are used in a flexible and efficient way to meet the demands of different sectors, while also reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

Some examples of sector coupling and Power-to-X applications include:

Power-to-Heat: using excess renewable electricity to produce heat for buildings or industrial processes, through technologies such as heat pumps or electric boilers.
Power-to-Cold: using excess renewable electricity to produce cooling for buildings or industrial processes, through technologies such as absorption chillers.
Power-to-Hydrogen: using renewable electricity to produce hydrogen through electrolysis, which can be used as a fuel for transportation or as a feedstock for industrial processes.
Power-to-Synfuels: using renewable electricity to produce synthetic fuels, such as methanol or synthetic natural gas, that can be used as substitutes for fossil fuels in transportation or industry.

By combining renewable energy sources with innovative technologies for energy conversion and storage, sector coupling and Power-to-X can help to create a more sustainable, reliable, and climate-neutral energy system.

1168. ID: 6089
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Beirut International
   Statement: ACTOR:
Beirut International - Marine Industry and Commerce sarl

CONTROVERSY:
The Danish “Energy Island” projects

TEXT:
Offshore wind energy generation is more efficient than on land, to harness it you’d have to follow the wind. Ocean water currents offer a much higher energy density, at a stable rate, the technology is progressing, to harness you’d have to follow the currents. 
To make Hydrogen Green, sea water reverse osmosis and electrolysis equipment have to be close to an energy source, from here the idea of Energy Islands begins. 

Energy Islands should be near the winds, waves and currents. The Baltic Sea average depth is 50 m, the North Sea 90 m, the Mediterranean Sea 1,500 m, the Atlantic Ocean 3,600 m.

Energy Islands should be accessible all year long. Offshore rigs personnel have to go through extensive safety training to be allowed to make the trip by Helicopter or by Offshore Support Vessels, both ways are expensive and at high risk.
Energy Islands should cater for additional space when an Wind Farm expands; and permit ergonomic maintenance and replacement of equipment without the use of heavy lift Floating Marine Cranes and Floating Docks.

Energy Islands service and operations teams may range from dozens to hundreds. This team require fresh water supply, food supply, cold service water, hot service water, wastewater disposal, solid waste disposal and regular rotation.  Offshore supply and retrieval trips made by Offshore Supply Vessels is dangerous and expensive in high seas.

Supposing a nation wishes to build an Energy Island by backfilling into the sea within its economic water zone; the currents within this sea would have to be studied not to alter direction and affect neighboring nations, the sediments from the backfilling process would be carried to undesirable locations within the nation shoreline, or to neighboring shoreline, affecting marine fauna and flora. A thorough Environmental Impact Assessment should be endorsed by all nation stakeholders.
Assuming an EIA is approved, lets look at the backfilling process on a sandy bed at 50 m seawater depth. If the surface footprint of the island is to be 500m x 500m, the scour protection measures, whatever the method used, would have a footprint of around 600m x 600m at sea bed level. The offshore contracting operations would have to be carried out within the yearly calm season, if the entire operation, or the milestone target construction is not achieved within the first season, the sea would destroy and remove most of it before the next season.
 After completion, if a structural failure occurs, under rough sea conditions, repairs would have to wait till the calm season, at the risk of further uncontrollable damage.
Once such Energy Island is completed, installing equipment on top would follow any port procedures; if certain components need to be replaced, they would have to be lifted and transported onto a vessel.
While this enormous offshore marine contracting job maybe concluded at 50m depth, will let the reader imagine the 90m or 1,500m sea depth scenario feasibility.

A Floating Island is fabricated in a shipyard, launched to sea, tugged to the desired location, and anchored. The process is carried in a controlled environment, irrespective of sea state and sea depth.
While many Floating Island solutions are marketed, and most developers submitted their design to the UN Habitat in 2018 in a New York meeting, none of their literature is conclusive, most of it is at conceptual level. 
The only solution that passed Two Marine Societies design approval by Bureau Veritas  in 2005 and International Naval Survey Bureau in 2009, and a thorough Marine Society design, engineering, procurement and fabrication survey by INSB from 2009 till 2015 is the one made by Dr. Abdullah Daou, the founder of Beirut International Marine Industry and Commerce. 
Beirut International’s Floating Island first prototype was made in 1997, at a scale of 1:10 measuring 4m x 4m, was extensively tested in a make shift water basin, with better than expected stability results under high simulated waves condition.

In 2009 the fabrication of the first Floating Island made by Beirut International started in Lebanon. The substructure base 48m wide, by 76m long, 9m deep and weighing around 4,000 tons was being assembled in Tripoli Shipyard, while structural components where being fabricated in three other workshops in Lebanon by a team of 431 local technicians and engineers. 
While the fate of this structure was unfortunate, Ninety-Eight Million US Dollars were invested in the research, development and fabrication; a 70% completion rate was achieved, almost all drawings approved and stamped by INSB meeting SOLAS and other marine regulations. 
The learning curve is priceless. The technology is ready, far ahead of any contender. True, a full-scale prototype is yet to be made again and tested.


There is seven pros for building the energy islands.
A Floating Energy Island is modular, making it scalable to meet any Offshore Wind Farm expansion. If maintenance is requires, a module can be detached, tugged to a shipyard then re-connected.
The substructure of a Floating Energy Island is transparent to the sea, making it an artificial coral reef for marine life, and simultaneously providing anchoring points to install Water Current Energy makers. 
The waves are absorbed and damped by the Floating Energy Island, creating a calm water area at the rear port for Vessel to approach and dock at ease, allowing for safe and friendly access. 
Being a generator of Hydrogen, and having a large underwater space, it is an ideal location to develop sustainable fisheries, creating an additional export income.
Solid waste composting and wastewater treatment available technologies can make some agriculture a sustainable alternative to waste disposal.
The Hydrogen process being noiseless, and clean; a Yacht Club can be safe haven for yachts sailing across seas and oceans.

However the cons of building the islands are yet to be tested by our firm.

The Hydrogen Environment is relatively new. 
Stakeholders include: Shipping Companies, Energy Companies, Ports Logistics, Telecommunication, Reverse Osmosis Water Makers, Electroliser Makers, Wind Turbine makers, Wave Energy Makers, Current Energy Makers, Shipyards, Marine Offshore Contractors, Hydrogen Storage Solution Makers, Inverters, Controls, Aquaponics, Wastewater Treatment, Solid Waste Treatment… 
While some stakeholders are more advanced then the other, some at prototyping stage, other at maturity; a Floating Energy Island success needs their close collaboration. A fresh firm in the Legal field is trying to advise stakeholders to join efforts and Joint Venture to make such infrastructure and energy concepts a needed reality to meet a Marine Decarbonization.

1169. ID: 1916
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Energinet
   Statement: We ensure that onshore balancing and reserve dimensioning align with the System Operation Guideline (SOGL) at both the LFC block and LFC area levels. We plan to apply the same principles for dimensioning and balancing to the future Danish energy islands. This means that each energy island will function as a separate LFC area within the same LFC block as the connected Danish onshore LFC areas.

By designating the energy islands as individual LFC areas, we enhance transparency regarding bottlenecks between the islands and the mainland while reducing the need for internal redispatch. Reserve dimensioning remains at the LFC block level, and the SOGL imposes no restrictions on sharing or exchanging reserves between LFC areas within the same block. Including the energy islands in the existing LFC block enables common reserve dimensioning for both the islands and the connected Danish onshore LFC areas.

Additionally, establishing new LFC areas supports the seamless integration of energy islands into European balancing platforms. However, there are legal challenges, as current legislation was drafted before the concept of energy islands existed. We believe that energy islands can be balanced under existing regulations, but legislative amendments are needed to explicitly cover small, isolated AC systems like the energy islands.

1184. ID: 2296
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Financial viability and (un)profitability
   Actor: John Ammentorp
   Statement: Energy islands are strategically vital and economically sound investments for several key reasons. The Danish North Sea energy island project will make energy more affordable by creating near-shore environments for far-offshore wind farms. By placing wind farms closer to energy islands instead of the mainland, the Danish North Sea energy island will reduce complexity and costs by minimizing or eliminating long underwater cable runs to shore.

Energy islands provide crucial flexibility in Denmark's renewable energy system. The Danish North Sea energy island will serve as an accumulation point for surplus energy during high-production periods and enable strategic distribution during peak demand times. This capability directly addresses the challenge of balancing renewable energy production with consumption.

The costs for the Danish North Sea energy island fall into three main categories:
1. Capital expenditures for physical infrastructure construction, including the artificial island itself and electrical infrastructure
2. Operational costs that vary based on design choices, technology selection, geographic location, and project scale
3. Technology development costs, particularly for high-voltage direct current equipment and Power-to-X systems

1189. ID: 1839
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Michael Stoltze
   Statement: The transition from climate-damaging to climate-neutral energy sources is fraught with challenges, including the massive scale of the required infrastructure. Bornholm’s geographical position in a critical sea area for renewable energy delivery to Northern Europe places the island in the middle of a significant dilemma.

While we recognize the uncertain economic feasibility of these large-scale projects, we are particularly concerned about their potential impact on Bornholm’s nature and landscape. These are foundational values for Bornholm and the main reasons for its popularity, which must not be jeopardized.

As Danmarks Naturfredningsforening Bornholm, our primary goal is to protect and improve nature, the environment, and the landscape. We fully support the green transition to a society that avoids pollution, stabilizes the climate, preserves nature, and protects landscapes. A blanket rejection of all development, including wind turbines and solar farms, is not a viable option. Effective environmental solutions are essential to address pollution and climate change while maintaining the integrity of nature and the landscape.

For the massive land-based energy infrastructure planned on Bornholm, we demand the highest standards and will not compromise. This will be the largest construction project in Bornholm’s history, occupying a small percentage of the island’s area but having a visible impact due to the height of the structures. Therefore, it must be situated in a way that minimizes harm to nature and the landscape. The design should incorporate architecture, vegetation, and earthworks to integrate harmoniously into the surroundings.

The proposed location north of Søndre Landevej, although not without issues, is the best option available. The site is primarily agricultural land with low natural value, flat terrain, and a location sufficiently distant from the scenic south coast. While the project will affect farmland and buildings, the surrounding natural environment can be enhanced through thoughtful design. The plan includes low vegetation, bushes, and trees between the buildings, as well as tree lines and the restoration of a small stream, which will increase the area’s biodiversity compared to its current state.

However, we emphasize the need for varied-height earthen berms around the site. These berms will reduce the visual dominance of the large buildings and provide habitats for diverse flora and fauna by creating microclimates. Additionally, the berms can be used for walking trails, offering both scenic views and access to nature.

Nature and the landscape must not be sacrificed. This project is a significant opportunity to develop a solution that benefits Bornholm while serving as a national and international model for integrating renewable energy development with respect for nature and the landscape. This is the challenge we face, and we are committed to making it a success.

1201. ID: 1841
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Søren Møller Christensen
   Statement: I have been asked several times how it makes sense to produce power-to-x on Bornholm. Wouldn't it make much more sense to transport electricity to Copenhagen or Berlin and convert it into, for example, jet fuels in those locations, where there are also large cities with extensive district heating networks that can absorb the significant amounts of heat? It’s a logical question.

The issue, however, is that transporting electricity through cables is expensive, while transporting hydrogen through pipelines is cheaper. In other words, from an economic perspective, it makes the most sense to produce hydrogen as close to the energy source as possible. This is reflected in the fact that wind turbine manufacturers are working on developing turbines that, in the future, will produce hydrogen directly inside the turbine or on platforms near the turbines. In these turbines, most of the heat will be lost, but they are expected to be cost-effective because the electricity is converted to hydrogen very close to the energy source.

However, this type of turbine will not be used for Energy Island Bornholm, as the primary focus is on electricity production, and the new turbine type is not expected to be ready until the 2030s.

Regarding the question of why it is relevant to produce hydrogen on Bornholm, it is also worth noting that Bornholm is not the only community grappling with what power-to-x means for them. Green fuels, particularly hydrogen, are part of the vision in most places where there are plans for major expansions of wind and solar energy—and often, these are in smaller communities far from major cities. For example, this is also the case for the two other energy islands in the Baltic Sea, Gotland and Åland. Åland, in particular, is far along in its plans to produce hydrogen based on the 4–6 GW of offshore wind that can be developed in the waters around the archipelago.

I am often asked whether power-to-x makes economic sense. The think tank Kraka has, for example, published a report arguing that building a power-to-x industry in Denmark will require substantial financial support because green fuels are currently more expensive than fossil fuels. Both the question and the argument are logical, but they do not change the fact that power-to-x is an essential part of the solution to the climate crisis. Moreover, there is political recognition of the need to find ways to enable the commercial production of green fuels.

This can happen through support from the Danish state or the EU, which is already occurring today. In the future, it is also expected to happen through additional taxes based on the amount of CO₂ emitted by a particular type of production, making CO₂-neutral fuels more competitive compared to, for instance, coal and oil.

Whether power-to-x is supported directly through subsidies or indirectly through CO₂ taxes, the energy sector expects power-to-x to play a crucial role in the green transition. Furthermore, there is significant political focus in Denmark on making power-to-x a new area of national industrial strength.

1219. ID: 5984
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Jacob Østergaard
   Statement: In collaboration with a range of other nations,
Denmark has committed to a massive increase in
renewable energy production. For the North Seas
alone, a 300 GW (Giga Watt) wind power capacity
has been agreed for 2050. In comparison, the total
Danish offshore wind power capacity today is 2.3 GW.
Meeting these commitments through near-shore
wind power parks alone will just not be possible.
Even if existing local planning and protests from
citizens were disregarded, the available space
would fall short by a large margin. Thus, the
build-out needs to be based on the use of the
open sea wind resource.
Fortunately, the potential for open sea wind power
production is huge. However, the technical setup
around near-shore wind power parks cannot be
transferred to the open sea. At today’s near-shore
parks, power is produced as an alternating current
(AC) and transmitted directly to shore. This would
not work for an open sea park. Due to the longer
distance, the power must be converted into a
direct current (DC). The space requirements for the
converters and related equipment demand housing
at a physical structure close to the production site.
In other words, a build-out of the scale in question
would be impossible without energy islands.

1232. ID: 1180
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Peter K. Kruse-Andersen
   Statement: I highlight a coordination problem between the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy. I exemplify this coordination failure by analyzing carbon leakage effects associated with Denmark's planned North Sea energy island. The Danish energy island project will not start production before 2033, implying a long interval between project announcement and production. Using a dynamic model of the EU ETS, I show that the large time gap between announcement and production likely results in a ‘Green Paradox’, where the energy island increases aggregate EU ETS emissions. The mechanism leading to the emission increase is complicated and works through the Market Stability Reserve (MSR). The estimated 2050 leakage rate is 145 percent in our main scenario and not below 100 percent in any alternative scenario. We discuss how to improve the climate benefits of the energy island or similar large-scale renewable energy projects. This includes possible revisions to the EU ETS and the role of Power-to-X technologies.

There is a coordination failure between the EU ETS and the EU's offshore renewable energy strategy, as projects intended to fulfil the offshore strategy are likely to result in substantial carbon leakage due to the EU ETS.
In ETS-covered sectors, there are averse leakage effects associated with emission abatement projects with significant time lags between project announcements and emission abatement like the Danish North Sea energy island.
For the North Sea energy island and similar projects, leakage effects can be diminished through policies that mitigate the impact on EU ETS allowance demand.
The coordination failure can be eliminated by removing MSR cancellations or the entire MSR mechanism while adjusting the emission cap to hold expected emissions constant.
However, removing MSR cancellations amplifies leakage effects for abatement projects with short time lags between announcements and emission abatement, which currently have weak leakage effects due to MSR cancellations.

1263. ID: 5598
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: Yes, it is true that both Energinet and the agreement group have approved the possibility of Chinese cables being used in Denmark, but this is contingent on the fulfillment of specific requirements. The upcoming offshore wind auctions will allow both European and non-European companies, including Chinese companies, to participate, provided they meet the tender conditions. However, the actual suppliers of components, such as cables, are not part of the auction process. The winner of the auction (the concessionaire) can select their own suppliers, including those of cables, for the wind farm construction.

For the future wind auctions, there will be conditions that must be met, including new access requirements. These will include compliance with social clauses, such as the obligation to provide apprenticeship opportunities and prevent social dumping. Furthermore, there will be requirements to adhere to human rights and international conventions. The principle of chain responsibility will also be introduced, meaning that the concessionaire will be accountable for ensuring both their own compliance and that of their suppliers when working in Denmark. Additionally, sustainability requirements will be enforced, such as ensuring that concessionaires obtain third-party verified environmental product declarations for key components, including cables, from their suppliers.

1268. ID: 1108
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute
   Statement: The southern part of the Baltic Sea supplies the central, deeper part of the Baltic Sea with saline and oxygen-rich water flowing from the Øresund and the Danish belts. Therefore, local impacts on the southern part of the Baltic Sea can affect the environment throughout the entire Baltic Sea. Several risks to the marine environment are associated with the cable laying. In sections where the submarine cable must be protected by rock deposits, increased turbulence could cause the bottom current to mix with water closer to the surface, reducing its quality and importance for the deep-water areas of the Baltic Sea. It is also essential for the Danish authorities to investigate and quantify how wind turbines affect ocean currents, waves, and the mixing of surface water.

1287. ID: 5694
   Year: 2023
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Andreas Wenzel
   Statement: The agreement encompasses a total of 9 gigawatts (GW) of offshore wind capacity, with the potential to expand to 14 GW or more. Currently, Denmark has 2.3 GW of offshore wind capacity in its waters. The agreement includes 6 GW of regular offshore wind farms and an additional 3 GW linked to the "Energy Island Bornholm Project." 

For the first time, the agreement establishes state co-ownership of offshore wind farms, with the Danish state and citizens holding a 20% stake. While this milestone is significant, it has sparked debates over the potential complexity and delays in the bidding process. The agreement sets a strict timeline for constructing the wind turbines by 2030.

The "Energy Island Bornholm Project" requires state support to be realized. Politicians have allocated up to 17.6 billion DKK in subsidies to cover the costs of an onshore facility on Bornholm and a high-capacity transmission cable connecting Bornholm, Zealand, and Germany. Germany will contribute its share and partially fund the onshore facility. However, the wind turbines themselves will be constructed without financial support.

This agreement represents a major step in the energy transition, ensuring the generation of significant amounts of green electricity for Denmark, Germany, and the rest of Europe.

1294. ID: 5360
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Belgium’s energy island
   Actor: Private person
   Statement: Belgium has started constructing the world’s first artificial energy island, Princess Elisabeth Island, located 45 kilometers off the Belgian coast in the North Sea. This project is a significant step forward in renewable energy infrastructure, aiming to enhance renewable energy usage and facilitate international energy exchange.  

The island, supported by a €100 million grant from the EU’s COVID-19 recovery fund, will feature integrated HVDC and HVAC systems to distribute energy from offshore wind farms to the grid. Hybrid interconnectors will enable connections with wind farms and energy trade between countries.  

The construction involves innovative methods, including 2.3 million cubic meters of sand and concrete caissons to form its base and walls. Strategically, this project reduces Belgium’s reliance on fossil fuels and positions the North Sea as a hub for Europe’s energy independence.  

The island’s physical structure is expected to be completed by 2026, with operations commencing in 2030. This groundbreaking initiative underscores Belgium’s leadership in renewable energy and its commitment to sustainability and energy security.

1307. ID: 5953
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: The Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Danish Energy Agency has reported on the socioeconomic impact assessments for different configurations of the Energy Island Bornholm under various scenarios. The Energy Island Bornholm project includes offshore wind farms, a transformer station on Bornholm, and grid connections to Denmark and Germany. Despite considerable uncertainty about future developments, the central socioeconomic estimates are negative across all scenarios, ranging from -4 billion DKK to -17 billion DKK.

The project is also expected to require public subsidies amounting to 31.5 billion DKK during the first approximately 20 years of the energy island's lifespan. Of this, 17.6 billion DKK was politically approved in May 2023. This approved subsidy will be financed through expected revenues from the auction of 6 GW offshore wind capacity (8.7 billion DKK), the Green Fund (4.9 billion DKK), and future fiscal space (4.0 billion DKK). An additional subsidy need of approximately 14 billion DKK has arisen due to the anticipated unprofitability of the offshore wind farms associated with the energy island, and no concrete financing has yet been identified for this amount.

Given the negative socioeconomic outlook, the Energy Island Bornholm project should be reconsidered. The socioeconomic assessment does not include several effects that are difficult to quantify, such as energy security and potential Power-to-X production. It is recommended that a comprehensive socioeconomic analysis be conducted, incorporating as many effects as possible. If it cannot be demonstrated that the project yields a socioeconomic surplus, the project should be abandoned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1309. ID: 5975
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Olga Lucia Uribe
   Statement: Hydrogen production through water electrolysis is a well-established and widely utilized process that has been successfully scaled and applied across various industries, both in Denmark and globally. Similarly, the production of ammonia, methanol, and the use of carbon dioxide (CO2) as a feedstock for fuel and chemical production are proven technologies. However, there is ongoing innovation in Power-to-X (PtX) technologies aimed at enhancing efficiency, reducing costs, and improving safety. These advancements focus on developing new catalysts, improving materials, and optimizing process integration to increase the viability and feasibility of PtX technologies.

The success of PtX projects depends on proper safety protocols and comprehensive risk assessments. These protocols address critical aspects such as the handling, production, storage, and transportation of fuels and chemicals. Risk assessments are crucial for identifying and mitigating potential vulnerabilities, reducing rework costs, ensuring regulatory compliance, and selecting appropriate security partners and protocols. Given the complexity of energy projects and the involvement of multiple stakeholders, these assessments form a foundational element for the successful and sustainable implementation of PtX initiatives. They help achieve project objectives while ensuring secure and efficient operations, ultimately advancing the overall potential of PtX technologies.

1348. ID: 5709
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Center for Regional and Tourism Research, Denmark
   Statement: We have studied the opportunities and challenges faced by communities like Bornholm when preparing for large energy projects. Our research adds depth to the debate on sustainable transition processes by focusing on local development shaped by these transitions. We emphasize that preparing for a green future involves not only building large-scale energy infrastructures but also transforming local communities. Local development must be prioritized for an inclusive and just transition. Our findings show that state-led investments like the Energy Island require significant structural changes at the local level, including vision-making, new business and education strategies, securing local interests, collaboration across administrative levels, new planning procedures, local engagement, and a strong communication strategy. These changes often involve reconfiguring the entire social ecosystem. While our findings are specific to Bornholm, they provide valuable insights for other regions with similar energy transition projects. We encourage systematic efforts to compare and report on these projects to better understand and navigate sustainability transitions.

   Statement: I hereby submit a legislative proposal to modify the investment screening law and gas supply law. The investment screening law changes introduce an earlier screening timeline for certain cases, specifically to enable greater parallel processing between the new EU foreign subsidy screening (FSR) and investment screening for offshore wind tenders and other major public energy projects.

These modifications are essential to avoid delays in upcoming tenders and reduce maintenance periods. For the investment screening law changes, adoption must occur in the current session to provide clarity to bidders and contracting authorities regarding the screening process and timing well before the bid deadlines for upcoming offshore wind tenders. This is particularly relevant as Energinet has already initiated tenders for electrical equipment for Energy Island Bornholm, with an expected bid deadline in autumn 2024.

Regarding the gas supply law changes, I propose introducing an explicit legal provision on the establishment and independence of the Energy Appeals Board to meet EU legal requirements under Article 41(17) of Directive 2009/73/EC and Article 60(8) of Directive (EU) 2019/944.

The proposal's late submission is due to the urgency of clarifying the screening process before the upcoming offshore wind tenders, including the already initiated Bornholm Energy Island electrical equipment tender. The law should enter into force on July 1, 2024.

This proposal does not entail significant economic consequences for businesses.

   Statement: Some of the consultation responses express concern about the impact on nature and local wildlife. According to the accompanying environmental report, much of the displaced animal and plant life during construction is expected to return once the facility is completed.

Earth embankments, trees, meadows, and vegetation between the station fence and residential areas will also help minimize potential visual disturbances.  

In addition to the local plan, an amendment to the existing municipal plan has been adopted. Together, the local plan and the municipal plan amendment establish the planning framework for the onshore facilities of Energy Island Bornholm. The next step is the consultation on the environmental assessment of the Energy Island, scheduled for late 2024.

1415. ID: 6919
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Sairoel Amertet Finecomess
   Statement: The newest innovation in energy management on the demand side is the smart meter, which helps reduce energy waste, improve productivity, and lower costs by monitoring energy consumption in real time. Smart meters allow users to easily and quickly track their energy usage, making them an innovative tool for energy management. These devices measure energy consumption in homes or businesses and communicate with the energy source to send data to the energy supplier, ensuring accurate billing. They also record usage data over time, enabling users to monitor consumption patterns and take steps to reduce energy use when necessary.

Smart meters can measure electricity, water, and natural gas usage and are typically connected to a wireless network for real-time data collection and transmission. By monitoring energy use in different areas of a home or business, users can identify specific areas of high consumption and take action to save energy. 

Smart meters offer several advantages. They provide consumers with real-time insights into their energy consumption, enabling cost-saving measures. Energy providers can use the data collected to create detailed profiles of customer energy usage, allowing for better demand management and more personalized services. The widespread adoption of smart meters in many countries is driving improvements in energy systems, enhancing efficiency, and empowering consumers with greater control and awareness of their energy use.

1432. ID: 5266
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: Kraka Economics
   Statement: The Energy Island Bornholm project is economically risky and underfunded. It has the potential to become a "slow-motion economic catastrophe." We recommend dropping the project before costs spiral out of control. 

Our analysis shows that the project is unlikely to attract bids to install offshore wind turbines because the expected income of 87 billion kroner from electricity sales over the project's lifespan is insufficient to cover costs unless the government increases the subsidy cap from 17.6 billion kroner to 31.5 billion kroner. Without this increase, the project is not financially attractive. 

To make the project viable with the current subsidy cap, electricity revenue would need to increase by 16.9 billion kroner, reaching 103.9 billion kroner. If the project were to proceed without any government support, the required revenue would rise to 125.3 billion kroner. This level of income is highly unlikely under current market conditions.

There is significant risk that the Energy Island Bornholm project cannot be realized within the current subsidy framework, and it is doubtful that companies will bid to install the wind turbines. If no bids are made, politicians face two choices: either abandon the project entirely or increase the subsidy to the necessary 31.5 billion kroner. While raising the subsidy might deliver the energy island, it contradicts the original intention of making the project economically self-sufficient.

Abandoning the project also carries financial consequences because the project is structured as smaller contracts. Terminating these contracts will result in substantial costs, even if the project ultimately fails to materialize. This financial risk makes it crucial to reconsider the feasibility of continuing with the Energy Island Bornholm project.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   Statement: Offshore wind, both fixed-bottom and floating, is crucial for the North Sea energy system, potentially contributing up to 51% of total power generation and reaching 498 GW of capacity by 2050. This technology also lowers the cumulative system cost of electricity and hydrogen by 4.21%. Fixed-bottom offshore wind will achieve 100% of its deployment potential regardless of technological learning and spatial planning. Senior economist Frederik Læssøe Nielsen from Kraka has publicly challenged proponents of the project to provide a single strong argument in favor of building the energy island. Key issues identified by Kraka include:  
- The substantial state subsidy requirement of at least 31.5 billion DKK.  
- No improvement to energy supply security from adding more wind turbines in the Baltic Sea.  
- Extremely high costs of producing Power-to-X (PtX) on Bornholm, as it is cheaper to produce PtX using other energy sources than offshore wind.  

Choosing nuclear power over Energy Island Bornholm could save Danish taxpayers a significant amount of money and offer a more viable energy solution.

Energinet, as the developer, is funding the archaeological work, which is being led by Bornholms Museum.

1523. ID: 5256
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Development & innovation opportunities on Bornholm
   Actor: Center for Regional and Tourism Research
   Statement: An analysis by CRT - Center for Regional and Tourism Research - concludes that Energy Island Bornholm has the potential to contribute significantly to reaching the political goal of 42,000 residents on Bornholm by 2030, but only if a Power-to-X facility is established.

CRT outlines three scenarios in its analysis:
1. **The Expected Scenario:** Represents the base case tied to Energy Island Bornholm’s construction and does not include any additional facilities or roles.
2. **The Possible Scenario:** Adds more jobs and new residents by making Bornholm an installation hub for offshore wind turbines during their construction phase, resulting in 100 additional jobs and 120 new residents.
3. **The Extended Scenario:** Builds upon the first two scenarios and introduces a Power-to-X facility on Bornholm, creating an additional 410 jobs and attracting 480 more residents.

In its calculations, CRT considers not only direct jobs created by the Energy Island project but also indirect effects, such as increased demand for local goods, restaurants, and childcare services. For example, Rønne Havn would need more staff to service wind turbines, and local businesses, such as food vendors, would hire additional employees to meet the rising demand.

Additionally, CRT estimates that there will be 5,300 temporary full-time equivalent positions created during the construction period leading up to 2030. However, CRT has not accounted for the long-term growth of the broader green industry on Bornholm, which could emerge from new business and research opportunities related to Energy Island Bornholm.

While it is impossible to quantify how many green companies and jobs might realistically develop as a result of these investments, CRT emphasizes that it is equally unrealistic to assume that no new energy-related businesses will emerge. Consequently, Energy Island Bornholm could create even more jobs than currently estimated.

1539. ID: 4847
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: LinkedIn user
   Statement: Regarding the proposed Vallø Energy Park:

The Green Citizens Group is opposed to the installation of solar panels and wind turbines in forests and open landscapes, especially in relation to the Vallø Energy Park, located south of Herfølge. Their concerns are summarized in their Facebook group, which include:
1. Negative impact on protected animal species and natural areas.
2. Noise pollution from massive wind turbines towering above the treetops.
3. Destruction of forested areas.
4. Devaluation of nearby properties.
5. Visual and noise disturbances from solar panels.

However, I do not believe the installation of wind turbines and solar panels will destroy the natural environment in this area. Vallø Energy Park is located in a production forest, as shown in the attached Google photo. The amount of forest felled annually will not increase due to the establishment of turbines in this area. A full environmental impact report will be prepared in the ongoing process to verify this.

One advantage of locating the energy park in a large forest area is the substantial distance between the project and nearby residents, ensuring that noise disturbance to local citizens is minimized. But this remains a sensitive issue, as public opinion on having turbines in Danish production forests is divided. A quick online search reveals many protests against the project, with a petition against it currently gathering 1,900 signatures. It's clear that the "nature argument" strongly resonates with people. 

In my view, however, whether the project actually harms nature is unlikely to be thoroughly investigated. The project will probably fail because politicians are afraid to go against public opinion. The large, silent majority that could support the project does not speak up.

The failure of many energy parks in recent years is a serious issue, as the Green Transition risks stalling. NIMBY (Not In My Back Yard) sentiment has always been a powerful force. Even regional politicians and some in Gentofte tried to stop the wind turbines at Middelgrunden, but only through a strong public mandate and a strategic alliance with Copenhagen Municipality were we able to convince Minister Svend Auken to approve the project. The bureaucracy and Danish Nature Conservation (DN) did everything they could to prevent the necessary permits from being granted.

Does Denmark truly need onshore energy parks? Yes, very much so. The illusory promises of Energy Islands and offshore wind farms are fading. To meet Denmark's overall energy needs, large-scale renewable energy (RE) is essential. All available tools must be used, and the Vallø Energy Park could be a significant step forward in this transition.

Without the onshore infrastructure, the wind turbines are essentially useless. Today’s approval is just one step in a long journey before the vision of Energy Island Bornholm becomes a reality.

1618. ID: 2221
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: The Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Danish Energy Agency has now taken a step further in the process with Energy Island Bornholm.

Based on the environmental assessment and received consultation responses, the Danish Energy Agency has just assessed that it is possible to adopt the Plan for the Energy Island Bornholm Program.

The plan sets the overall framework for the upcoming construction projects related to Energy Island Bornholm and off the coast.

This is stated by the Danish Energy Agency in a press release.

Energy Island Bornholm will consist of an offshore wind farm south of Bornholm as well as high-voltage facilities on Bornholm and Zealand. The energy island will have a total capacity of up to 3.8 GW.

According to the plan, the offshore wind turbines can have a total height of up to 330 meters.

The plan alone does not allow for the establishment of facilities, but the Danish Energy Agency is currently preparing the upcoming tender for offshore wind, they state in the announcement.

The plan describes where both the offshore facility, with wind turbines and sea cables in the Baltic Sea and the Øresund, will be located, as well as where the two onshore facilities on Bornholm and Zealand will be built with the landing of cables and high-voltage facilities.

Energy Island Bornholm is growing
With the Climate Agreement for Energy and Industry etc. 2020 on June 22, 2020, it was decided that Denmark will realize two energy islands – one in the North Sea and one on Bornholm. The climate agreement was concluded by the then S-government, Venstre, the Danish People's Party, the Social Liberal Party, the Socialist People's Party, the Red-Green Alliance, the Conservative People's Party, the Liberal Alliance, and the Alternative.
In 2022, the then government and the agreement circle reached an agreement to expand Energy Island Bornholm from 2 to 3 GW.
In the spring of 2023, the current government and the agreement circle reached a supplementary agreement that sets the tender framework for the 3 GW at Energy Island Bornholm with the possibility of 800 MW overplanting.
In parallel with the work of the Danish Energy Agency, Energinet, which is the developer for the onshore facilities of Energy Island Bornholm, has carried out an environmental assessment process for the facilities on Zealand and Bornholm as well as sea cables between the two station facilities.

The sea cables will connect the offshore wind farms with the high-voltage facility on Bornholm and connect the high-voltage facility on Bornholm with the transmission network in Zealand and Germany, it states.

The Danish Energy Agency states that in the process with Energy Island Bornholm, they have made a number of spatial adjustments to the planning areas to "accommodate environmental conditions and land use constraints in the area, such as bird protection areas, defense areas, and shipping routes," it says.

Here the Danish Energy Agency has pointed out
On Bornholm, the Danish Energy Agency has pointed out an area of 1340 hectares for the establishment of a high-voltage facility and land cables. The area is located in the southern part of Bornholm about one km south of Nylars, Lobbæk, and Aakirkeby. Land cables will be established along the same stretch.
In Zealand, electricity from Energy Island Bornholm can be connected to the existing 400 kV electricity transmission network at Solhøj. The exact location of a high-voltage facility for this purpose depends on the permits that can be obtained from Ishøj and Høje Taastrup municipalities.
The landing will take place either at Vallø Strand in Køge Municipality, the coast in Stevns Municipality, or at Karlstrup Strand in Solrød Municipality.
A total of 35.3 km of land area has been identified where land cables can be established.
As part of the planning and environmental assessment process, the Danish Energy Agency has held a number of public meetings in 2021, 2022, and 2023, where citizens, stakeholders, and authorities have submitted ideas, proposals, concerns, and asked questions about the draft plan and environmental assessment.

If you do not agree with the Danish Energy Agency's approval of the plan, you can appeal to the Energy Appeals Board until June 10.

1620. ID: 2213
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: LinkedIn user
   Statement: Energy Island Bornholm

The text below is the introduction to my note on Energy Island Bornholm. You can no longer attach a file or a link to posts on LinkedIn, but I am happy to send the entire note to those interested.

Energy Island Bornholm is intended to pave the way for Denmark to maintain its leading position as a green pioneer country. The Economic Council has warned about the project's poor economic viability. An article in Jyllands-Posten on December 25, 2024, highlights the benefits that are not included in the economic analyses, including Denmark's technological leadership, the path to new international electricity connections, supply security, and job creation on Bornholm. These are airy and well-known arguments. When trying to gain a more concrete understanding of the project, it turns out to be wrapped in many words but with few useful details. This is especially true for the project's technical design. My conclusions about Energy Island Bornholm:

It is a serious democratic problem that parts of the documentation for such a large public investment are kept secret.
There is almost no publicly available information about the chosen technical solutions. This prevents technically interested parties from assessing the project's technical risks.
Since Energinet's "Business case" from 2022, the expectation of the project's economic viability has significantly deteriorated. Therefore, it must be decided whether the project should be changed or abandoned.
The choice of an energy island over a platform solution results in the concentration of large energy transactions in a few points, thereby increasing the vulnerability of the electricity supply in Denmark and the rest of Europe. In light of increased international tensions, this choice should be reconsidered.
The technical interconnection on the energy island is described in Energinet's risk assessment as "immature." This is an understatement, as the interconnection is challenging and has so far only been attempted on a full scale in very few places in the world.
No Danish companies develop or produce HVDC equipment, so it serves no Danish interest to rely on untested solutions. Multiterminal offshore HVDC solutions should not be included in the project in any form until the necessary new technologies are fully tested elsewhere.
Analyses of alternative solutions have been neglected. Due to poor economics and technological uncertainty, the project should be put on hold until all relevant solutions are properly investigated and evaluated.

1629. ID: 2163
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: I have obtained contributions from the Danish Energy Agency to answer the question. The Danish Energy Agency informs: “Energinet, as a state-owned company, is responsible for the overall infrastructure in the electricity and gas sectors, according to the Energinet Act. Therefore, Energinet has planned for the connection of Energy Island Bornholm to the Zealand electricity grid. In Energinet’s planning, four possible connection points were assessed based on objective evaluation criteria, namely three existing 400 kV stations – Hovegård, Avedøre, and Bjæverskov – and a new station west of Copenhagen in the 400 kV grid at the branching point towards Copenhagen, later referred to as Station Solhøj. Energinet states that the following criteria were used for the overall assessment:
• Identification of derived grid limitations and the need for internal grid reinforcements
• The technical design of the project and the economic consequences of connecting the cable to Bornholm
• Considerations regarding the size of the potential land area, landscape conditions, extent of other buildings, need for purchasing/demolition of homes
• Technical consequences for the electricity system in terms of stability and robustness
• Possibility of co-location, e.g., placement of future PtX facilities
• Perspectives for the long-term development of the energy system
The assessment was based on the applicable analysis assumptions, specifically AF20. Based on an overall assessment of the four options, Energinet chose a new station, Solhøj, in 2021. Expansion of the existing stations at Avedøre and Hovegård was considered but rejected, according to the evaluation criteria above. Hovegård was rejected as it was assessed that it would not provide the same flexibility as Solhøj in connection with potential future grid expansions. Furthermore, connecting at Hovegård would require an expansion of the station in an area with more buildings and infrastructure than the existing station. Hovegård is geographically located somewhat less favorably in relation to integration with district heating and other infrastructure. Avedøre was rejected as it was assessed that Avedøre Power Plant as a connection point for Energy Island Bornholm is the most risky. Depending on whether associated electricity consumption is established alongside the connection of Energy Island, this would require one or two 400 kV reinforcements. Additionally, it is assessed that connecting Energy Island at Avedøre Power Plant could cause stability issues.” The former Minister approved Energinet’s recommendation in October 2022 regarding the Energy Bornholm eInfrastructure project, including the establishment of Station Solhøj, which is necessary for the grid connection of Energy Island Bornholm. The Minister also informed the KEF committee of the approval at the same time. The former Minister for Climate, Energy, and Utilities also requested in September 2022 that the then Minister for the Interior and Housing provide planning grounds for the grid connection of Energy Island Bornholm. As a result, a process has been initiated to prepare a national planning directive.

1652. ID: 2136
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: The Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Danish Energy Agency (Energistyrelsen) has assessed the socio-economic consequences of various configurations of the Bornholm Energy Island project, which includes wind farms, a transformer station on Bornholm, and grid connections to Denmark and Germany. The central estimates for the socio-economic impact across all scenarios are negative, with potential losses ranging from 4 billion DKK to 17 billion DKK.
Additionally, the project is expected to require public subsidies amounting to 31.5 billion DKK over the first approximately 20 years of operation. Of this amount, 17.6 billion DKK has already been politically approved as of May 2023. The approved funding will be sourced from anticipated revenues from the 6 GW offshore wind tender (8.7 billion DKK), the Green Fund (4.9 billion DKK), and future fiscal space (4.0 billion DKK).
However, an additional subsidy of approximately 14 billion DKK is needed because the wind farms associated with the energy island are not expected to be profitable, and no specific financing has been identified for this amount.
Given the negative socio-economic outlook, the project should be reconsidered. The current socio-economic assessment does not account for several effects that are difficult to quantify, such as energy supply security and potential Power-to-X production. Therefore, it is recommended that a new socio-economic analysis be conducted, incorporating as many relevant effects as possible.
