1661. ID: 1835
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Helle Munk Ravnborg
   Statement: Dear Erik Kryger.

Of course, we need to be able to store the surplus energy generated when the wind is strong and the sun is shining in a clear sky, so that we can use that energy later during calmer and cloudier periods. This is part of what the development of future energy systems is about. Fortunately, many initiatives are underway to make this possible. Currently, battery storage and thermal storage—i.e., using electricity to heat water, and perhaps soon salt as well—are among the best and most energy-efficient solutions. In areas with significant elevation differences, pumped hydro storage is also an option—and development is progressing rapidly!

For example, I recently read that in California, batteries charged mainly by solar power are now the primary source of electricity during peak demand periods. Previously, natural gas was the main source during those hours. In other words, hydrogen production is by no means necessary to make use of the excess electricity generated on windy or sunny days when the grid cannot absorb it. There are alternative solutions, and they are even much more energy-efficient.

However, I suspect it is not entirely accurate to say that the primary goal of what you refer to as "the commercial ideas behind hydrogen production" is to ensure maximum utilization of surplus wind energy. The hydrogen projects planned for Bornholm are clear evidence of this.

For instance, in connection with the Energy Island Bornholm project, there is talk of “overplanting” by 800 MW (!). In other words, the goal is to produce substantial amounts of electricity, even though it’s already known that the grid cannot absorb it. Until recently, plans for an additional 3 GW of offshore wind capacity near Bornholm were solely for hydrogen production. It is in the context of such projects that I believe it is crucial for us as a society, and as responsible policymakers, to consider whether hydrogen production on Bornholm is a sensible path to take—because there is indeed a price to be paid.

Wind turbines must be manufactured and installed. Cables must be laid. Properties must be expropriated. Industrial facilities must be built, not only to establish the electrolysis plants but also to supply the water needed for splitting into hydrogen and oxygen at the required volume and purity (“technical” water). Then, infrastructure must be created to either transport the hydrogen elsewhere or convert it further into methanol (which requires capturing CO₂ that will be re-released when the methanol is burned) or ammonia. All this requires both resources and capital. And let’s be honest: the capital invested will also need to generate returns.

Therefore, it is crucial for these hydrogen projects to find ways to profit from the significant energy losses associated with hydrogen production—essentially, to monetize the heat generated by the process. If this doesn’t happen, the subsidies that you, I, and other taxpayers are already paying to this hydrogen industry—without being consulted—will have to increase even more. These are already considerable amounts of money being funneled into this sector via Danish and European funds.

In other words, we will end up paying for the energy losses—either through the cost of so-called “surplus heat” for radiators, swimming centers, greenhouses, or whatever else people imagine, or through subsidies to the energy companies, private equity firms, and pension funds involved in hydrogen production. Frankly, I struggle to see the benefit of this—either economically or environmentally.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1672. ID: 2132
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: COWI
   Statement: COWI: 

COWI supports the development of the "Jammerbugt Go Green" onshore energy island project. This project includes a solar park, an energy cluster, and facilities such as a biogas plant with CO₂ capture, a grass protein plant, and Power-to-X (PtX) plants for producing hydrogen and e-methanol. COWI highlights the symbiotic integration of the energy island with local agriculture, businesses, residents, and nearby wind turbines.  

Unlike standalone energy projects, the energy island offers the advantage of interconnecting various energy technologies in an industrial symbiosis, facilitating resource recycling of biomass, nutrients, biogenic CO₂, water, and electricity. The energy cluster is central to this symbiosis, with facilities located close together to ensure short connections for efficient processes and to concentrate environmental impacts away from nearby neighbors.  

The energy cluster is expected to operate year-round, 24/7, although some components may pause during nighttime or for balancing or operational reasons. Electricity for the energy cluster will be sourced from the project's solar panels and nearby wind turbines. These sources will be directly connected to the cluster via a dedicated transformer station. The station will also connect to Denmark's electricity grid, enabling energy exchange when beneficial. However, the energy island is designed to be net self-sufficient in electricity, including power from the local wind turbines, which are owned and operated by another developer.

1673. ID: 2128
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Energinet, Bornholms Municipality
   Statement: The high-voltage station contains components with oil, but these components are sealed. In the event of a leak, any oil release will be contained by the underlying concrete floor. Similarly, in the rare event of a transformer fire, the concrete floor will prevent any spillage. Fires in transformers are extremely rare and have never occurred in modern converter buildings enclosed in concrete. 

If a fire were to occur, standard safety protocol dictates allowing the facility to burn down without attempting to extinguish the fire. This ensures no contamination from extinguishing water. The risk to groundwater from an oil-related incident is negligible due to the low permeability of the clay-rich upper soil layers and the depth of over 40 meters to the groundwater extraction layers. This depth significantly delays potential contamination, providing ample time for cleanup. 

Additionally, groundwater flow is directed toward the sea, meaning the groundwater beneath the project area flows away from the nearest waterworks wells located to the northwest. Consequently, there is no risk of impacting drinking water production.

1693. ID: 149
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: If we do not have the international connections via energy islands as originally envisioned with Energy Island Bornholm and Energy Island North Sea, then the Danish energy supply security is expected to face challenges leading up to and after 2030. This is outlined, among other things, in the Climate Program 2024. The government expects to address this challenge in a proposal on electricity supply security.

There are generally several different ways to ensure a stable electricity supply. Electricity trade over international connections can balance capacity challenges between price zones; controllable electricity production capacity, which is not weather-dependent, can ensure production when fluctuating energy sources are not producing; storage technologies can, for example, store electricity when production is high and return it to the system during shortages; and technical and market solutions for consumption flexibility can ensure that electricity consumption aligns with production or, for instance, shifts to times when production is high. These measures complement each other and do not necessarily stand alone.

1703. ID: 123

   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: The Program Plan for the Bornholm Energy Island establishes the framework for the upcoming energy island on Bornholm and its surrounding waters. The energy island will consist of an offshore wind farm south of Bornholm and high-voltage infrastructure on Bornholm and Zealand. The energy island is expected to have a capacity of up to 3.8 GW and will play a vital role in phasing out fossil energy sources.

During the process, the Danish Energy Agency made spatial adjustments to planning areas to address environmental concerns and spatial constraints, including bird protection areas, defense zones, and shipping routes.

The Danish Energy Agency also held public meetings in 2021, 2022, and 2023 during consultation periods, where citizens, stakeholders, and authorities submitted ideas, proposals, concerns, and questions regarding the draft plan and environmental assessment. The plan sets the overarching framework for future construction projects related to the Bornholm Energy Island.

The plan itself does not authorize the construction of facilities. The decision by the Danish Energy Agency can be appealed to the Energy Appeals Board within a four-week period ending on June 10, 2024.

At the same time, Denmark and the rest of Europe face an overwhelming challenge: building affordable and reliable energy supplies, an issue that has become more urgent than meeting climate targets. This failed tender also has severe implications for other energy plans, including the two proposed "Energy Islands" in the North Sea and on Bornholm. The North Sea Energy Island has been postponed indefinitely due to high costs, and Energy Island Bornholm, which was already predicted to be unprofitable, must now also be considered financially untenable. The 8.7 billion kroner required for its construction was supposed to come from revenues from offshore wind in the North Sea.

It was a grave mistake to rely almost exclusively on offshore wind. It was unwise to embrace wind turbines with such blind faith while rejecting alternative solutions like nuclear power, which Denmark's Social Democrats have opposed for decades in pursuit of CO2-neutral energy. Now, everyone is left to suffer from the consequences of this failure, and we all know who will ultimately foot the bill for this debacle.

   Statement: The debate about Energy Island Bornholm lacks perspective. This project is not just about Bornholm.  

Energy Island Bornholm represents a transformative initiative with three key pillars: climate impact, industrial leadership, and geopolitical security. It is critical for Denmark and Europe to maintain a visionary approach to transition away from fossil fuels, ensuring a greener and more secure future.  

Firstly, Energy Island Bornholm serves as a catalyst for the green transition, not only by delivering green electricity to 3-4 million households and reducing CO₂ emissions by over 3 million tons annually but also by spearheading innovations for future energy islands. In particular, its role supports Europe's ambitious goal of 300 GW offshore wind by 2050, making such targets achievable cost-effectively.  

Secondly, this project secures Denmark’s technological and industrial leadership in green energy, especially wind technology. By acting as a test and innovation platform, it ensures Danish companies remain at the forefront of energy island development, safeguarding their competitive edge in global markets.  

Thirdly, from a security perspective, Energy Island Bornholm reduces Europe's dependency on Russian oil and gas by enhancing energy self-reliance. It is a vital infrastructure for connecting Baltic and European electricity markets and scaling offshore wind energy in the North Sea.  

Criticisms of Energy Island Bornholm’s economic viability often fail to consider the broader societal and strategic benefits. While the Energy Agency’s 2023 calculations show a potential deficit of 4 billion DKK, this does not account for key value drivers, including Denmark’s leadership in wind technology, potential revenue from international energy connections (e.g., a cable to Poland estimated to improve economics by 15-20 billion DKK), and expected EU funding.  

Additional benefits like energy security, job creation, Power-to-X production, and Bornholm's economic integration further underscore the project’s importance. Energy Island Bornholm is a long-term investment in critical infrastructure, with the potential to generate economic growth, strengthen Denmark’s position as a wind energy leader, and support Europe’s green and security agendas.

   Statement: The original arguments for Energy Island Bornholm, such as promises of an export boom and massive revenues, have largely fallen apart. As a result, supply security has increasingly become the central justification for the project. However, this is insufficient to offset the poor socio-economic viability.  

The latest profitability analysis shows a socio-economic deficit of 7 billion DKK, and this deficit is likely to have grown due to the recent delay in the tender process for the wind turbines.  

By comparison, a conservative estimate places the benefits of improved supply security at around 3 billion DKK, which is far from enough to balance the socio-economic loss. Moreover, the primary contributor to supply security is the cable to Germany, which could almost certainly be implemented more cheaply without routing through Bornholm.  

Therefore, Danish supply security is a weak argument for the project.  

Energy Island Bornholm does contribute to European supply security, making this a political decision. Politicians should openly acknowledge this and be transparent with voters that Danish taxpayers are being asked to fund the energy security of wealthier neighboring countries.

1746. ID: 34
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Kraka Economics
   Statement: Kraka Economics views the lack of bids for 3 GW of offshore wind in the North Sea as a political and structural failure but also as an opportunity to reset Denmark’s approach to the green transition. Kraka Economics recommends the following actions to rectify the situation and improve future renewable energy projects:

1. Simplify the Auction Design: Design a simpler and more conventional tender process that avoids imbalanced responsibilities and places financial accountability for delays on the responsible party. The tender should allow bidders to compete for both contributions to the state and subsidies, creating a fair market test.

2. Eliminate State Ownership: State ownership in offshore wind is unnecessary and complicates the process. Politically driven models, such as partial state ownership with minimal influence, add confusion for developers. Instead, Denmark can capture economic gains through taxation or during the tender process without operating as a minority owner.

3. Coordinate Supply and Demand: Align auctions with clear plans for hydrogen pipelines and Power-to-X (PtX) infrastructure. Market actors have long called for integrated planning rather than the current disjointed approach, which wastes resources and creates inefficiencies.

4. Stabilize Auction Timelines: Conduct tenders at a steady pace aligned with market demand to avoid bottlenecks and ensure the industry has confidence in a predictable long-term strategy.

Kraka Economics criticizes Denmark’s Climate, Energy, and Utilities Minister Lars Aagaard for downplaying the failures of the tender process despite longstanding warnings of its flaws. Kraka Economics urges the government to take proactive leadership to correct these issues rather than continuing to overlook them.

Finally, Kraka Economics emphasizes that tenders remain the optimal approach for renewable energy expansion. Even if offshore wind requires subsidies, tenders should be used to determine the level of support while also evaluating how much capacity Denmark should develop for export to Europe.

These adjustments, Kraka Economics argues, will create a more efficient, cost-effective, and reliable framework for Denmark’s green transition.

1748. ID: 85
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Hanne Storm Edlefsen
   Statement: I understand that Bornholm residents want to benefit from the Energy Island, particularly in terms of consuming and producing green electricity on the island. Our analysis shows that it is both technically feasible and a sound socio-economic solution. However, the establishment of the Energy Island will not result in lower electricity prices locally for Bornholm. 

Electricity prices in Denmark have been relatively stable until recent fluctuations caused by the war in Ukraine. As part of the Energy Island project, we are creating a third bidding zone, DK3, which will apply to Bornholm. This new zone will act as a marketplace for electricity produced and sold on Bornholm. It will include the facilities associated with the Energy Island and the local electricity grid currently operated by Trefor.

The creation of DK3 will give Bornholm residents access to the electricity produced on the island, resulting in relatively stable prices without significant fluctuations. This stability is due to Bornholm’s location between Denmark and Germany, where electricity prices are often similar, and the island’s consistent electricity production from its favorable wind conditions.

1752. ID: 76
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Danish Energy Agency
   Statement: After our thorough environmental assessment and review of consultation responses, we at the Danish Energy Agency have approved the Plan for Program Energiø Bornholm. The energy island project can now move forward.

The plan establishes the framework for building an energy island that will include offshore wind farms south of Bornholm and high-voltage installations on both Bornholm and Zealand. This facility will deliver up to 3.8 GW capacity, marking a significant step in Denmark's transition away from fossil fuels.

In developing the plan, we have made specific spatial adjustments to accommodate environmental protections, defense requirements, and shipping routes. These adjustments ensure the project respects bird protection areas and other critical zones.

Our planning process has been highly consultative, with multiple citizen meetings held between 2021 and 2023. We have actively gathered and incorporated input from citizens, stakeholders, and authorities regarding both the draft plan and its environmental assessment.

While this approved plan establishes the overall framework, it does not itself authorize construction to begin. Our decision can be appealed to the Energy Complaints Board until June 10, 2024.

   Statement: Based on this study, Offshore Energy Islands (OEIs), when integrated into the European North Sea grid with electrolyser flexibility, can significantly reduce grid costs for connecting offshore turbines to the coast and inland routes. 1791. ID: 877
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Giles Dickson
   Statement: The failure of the Danish offshore wind auction is not surprising, but it is certainly disappointing. The main issue lies with Denmark’s auction design, which lacks a revenue stabilization model or state support, unlike a Contracts for Difference (CfD) scenario. As a result, developers are left paying merely for the rights to build a wind farm, with the uncapped negative bidding process driving up costs and risk. Additionally, bidders are burdened with high upfront costs and grid connection expenses. The Danish Government needs to overhaul its auction design. Most other European countries use 2-sided CfDs in their offshore wind auctions, which provide more stability. WindEurope recommends that the 3GW be re-tendered in the April 2025 auction and urges the government to adapt its auction design before then.

1809. ID: 329
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Moderaterne
   Statement: The expected low market prices are the main reason no one is bidding. Today's auction format consists of three components: 1) the bidder pays a fee per kWh to get the construction rights, 2) the state will own 25% of the wind farm, 3) the builder's (owner's) economy depends on future market prices for electricity.

One can naturally bid zero øre for the fee per kWh, so that is not the explanation for the lack of bids. The requirement for the state to own 25% can be difficult to swallow for various reasons. Some may not have a problem with it, while others dislike it on principle.

The simple explanation for the lack of bids is that bidders do not believe that market prices over the next 15 years will be high enough to cover financing, operation, and maintenance.

This expectation of low future electricity prices is good news for all electricity customers, but when the auction system prevents new electricity from being built, it is very bad news for the climate and ultimately for the general public.

It was the Moderates who advocated for the new auction format, likely because it is more market-oriented/capitalistic than previous auction formats (though sweetened with state ownership).

In conclusion, the Danish government must acknowledge that a poor auction format was chosen, and a new (actually old) auction type, such as "strike price," must be selected, and a new auction must be conducted as soon as possible.

Additionally, the costs include long cables, backup power when the wind isn't blowing, and economically unrealistic projections for Power-to-X (PtX) technology.

In 2023, wind power across 13 northwestern European countries ranged from 5.6 GW to 121 GW, with an average of 46 GW and a standard deviation of 52% of the average. 

Wind power should be recognized as viable only to a very limited extent. It's time to stop looking to the misguided idealists from 40-50 years ago, who stood in front of Christiansborg Palace and sang: "What should go in? Sun and wind! What should go out? Barsebæk!" 

We ended up with 20 wind turbines at Middelgrunden, with a total capacity of 40 MW and an average output of 8.8 MW in 2023, varying between 14 MW in October and 4.1 MW in June. Such variation significantly limits the usefulness of wind power, which led us to build an 800-900 MW power plant at Avedøre to replace Barsebæk. This plant still emits some carbon dioxide, so it wasn't exactly a green transition.

In contrast, other offshore wind projects can be built without subsidies, and revenues from the upcoming 6 GW offshore wind auction are being earmarked to cover Energiø Bornholm’s deficit. 

Despite these financial challenges, Energinet initiated tenders for high-voltage equipment and cable installations in late 2023. This ongoing tender process is highly risky, as entering multiple contracts with bidders will incur significant penalties if the project exceeds the subsidy cap and has to be canceled.

Three scenarios are possible:  
1. The project miraculously stays within the subsidy cap, resulting in an energy island costing 17.6 billion DKK, with two-thirds of its electricity exported to Germany.  
2. The project exceeds the subsidy cap and is canceled, leaving Danish taxpayers with a substantial bill from the terminated tenders but avoiding the costly energy island.  
3. The project exceeds the subsidy cap, and politicians abandon their commitment to the cap, approving financing for a 31.5 billion DKK energy island—twice the cost per GW compared to the paused North Sea energy island project.

None of these outcomes are favorable for Danish taxpayers. Our clear recommendation to politicians is to cancel Energiø Bornholm before costs spiral out of control.

1834. ID: 394

   Statement: The lack of connection to mainland grids results in smaller, more isolated grids. Even where there is interconnection, it can be a single cable, making the entire grid very vulnerable to outages.
The irony is that islands have readily available renewable resources. From tidal to wind, solar, hydro, geothermal and biomass, islands offer renewable options and if you explore the specifics of each island, you will find that there is always a path to more renewable energy use, energy independence and climate neutrality.
We were able to demonstrate how small, water-scarce islands can use limited renewable energy to desalinate brackish water or seawater, reducing the need for CO2-intensive water tankers and providing people with climate-neutral water.
In Madeira, INSULAE investigated the use of novel smart charging technologies and electric vehicle grid integration to smooth energy demand. We proved how electric vehicle grid integration, where energy from an electric vehicle’s battery is fed back into the electricity grid, can help island grids manage the peaks and valleys of energy consumption, especially considering the expected increase in electricity demand due to the electrification of transport,..
INSULAE's research and technological developments clearly demonstrate the technical and economic feasibility of decarbonising and decentralising the energy supply of islands. I am confident that our work will ultimately provide islands with greater autonomy in terms of energy supply and security, while reducing energy costs and, most importantly, CO2 emissions.

1837. ID: 358
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Researchers
   Statement: The expansion of the political target to 70 GW of offshore wind in Germany compared to the old German grid development plan (NEP) will lead to an extreme increase in grid costs in order to integrate this higher amount of wind power into the German electricity market. For this reason, the task of this study is to examine the economic advantages and disadvantages of direct use of offshore electricity (e.g. through electromobility, heat pumps and new industrial processes) compared to hydrogen production with electricity from offshore wind.
The results show that Offshore Energy Islands (OEIs), taking into account meshing in the European North Sea grid and electrolyser flexibility, can contribute to the following aspects: Firstly, this results in savings in grid costs both for connecting offshore turbines to the coast and for inland routes. Secondly, they enable efficient hydrogen production without long transportation routes for the electricity. Thirdly, in times of low offshore wind and high solar PV generation, connecting the OEIs on the electricity side can make it possible to convert the surplus solar PV electricity into hydrogen.
In this study, a scenario with two OEIs connected to the electricity grid results in annuity savings of 4261 MEUR/yr, which is especially due to possible savings in HVDC cables.

1847. ID: 3719

   Cluster: Energy islands as a cornerstone in Europe’s green transition
   Actor: Glenda Napier
   Statement: The concept of energy islands is the opposite of isolation; they are essential, interconnected hubs for the green energy future of Denmark and Europe. Energy islands will serve as critical infrastructure, distributing green electricity from offshore wind farms to millions of households across Northern Europe, aiding the transition to CO2 neutrality.

Although the timeline for the North Sea Energy Island has been extended to 2036, this delay highlights the complexity and groundbreaking nature of the task rather than diminishing its importance. Energy islands demand innovative solutions and cross-sector collaboration, including partnerships between research institutions and industries.

Key questions we address include: Can hydrogen and electricity be transmitted through a single cable? How should transformer stations be optimally placed? Is it more efficient to transport AC or DC power? How can we meet GridCode requirements while ensuring stability and resistance to disruptions? Additionally, energy islands must integrate technologies like Power-to-X to convert surplus energy into green hydrogen, supporting stable grid operations and resource efficiency.

Through the Offshore Energy Hubs project, researchers from DTU, Aalborg University, Siemens Gamesa, Ørsted, and other partners are developing technologies to make energy islands more reliable and cost-effective. These innovations are already generating significant interest, both nationally and internationally.

Energy Cluster Denmark plays a pivotal role in facilitating innovation in the energy sector. By bringing together stakeholders from academia, industry, and government, we ensure that the best knowledge and technologies are applied to projects like energy islands. Competent partnerships are crucial; no energy island can succeed without collaboration across universities, companies, authorities, and nations.

We encourage all who have expertise and energy to contribute to climate-friendly solutions to engage with Energy Cluster Denmark and join initiatives like Offshore Energy Hubs. The green transition requires action, innovation, and strong partnerships. At Energy Cluster Denmark, we are ready to lead the way.

1876. ID: 4681

   Statement: The six gigawatts of offshore wind energy capacity being tendered are divided into two phases. The first phase, comprising three gigawatts across three offshore wind farms in the North Sea, had its bid deadline on Thursday at 14:00. The second phase, comprising three gigawatts across three wind farms in Denmark's inner waters, has a bid deadline of April 1, 2025. The tender is structured as a subsidy-free auction where energy companies must pay the state for the right to produce wind energy. Additionally, the Danish state will own a 20 percent share in each wind farm. The tender also allows for overplanting, enabling energy companies to build wind farms with capacities exceeding the minimum requirements. This could potentially increase the total capacity of the projects to 10 gigawatts or more, provided there are sufficient bids from energy companies.

1889. ID: 3561
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Reddit user
   Statement: Offshore wind provides an accessible and straightforward way to add significant gigawatts of renewable power, as it bypasses land and permitting challenges. However, solar remains cheaper for daytime energy production, and onshore wind is easier to integrate into the grid and less expensive to install.

Almost every location near offshore wind can still benefit significantly from solar energy, which can supply all daytime power during certain seasons. Historically, solar energy also commands the highest rates during peak times of the day.

In many areas, particularly those close to offshore wind farms, adding more renewables to the grid can lead to curtailments or periods of low wholesale energy prices during times of peak demand, which results in lower revenue projections for projects. Offshore wind is far less predictable than solar, despite having higher capacity factors.

Direct-to-Hydrogen (H2) solutions not only provide a much cheaper transmission option for offshore wind energy, but also allow for more affordable energy development far offshore. It offers certain project monetization, as it isn’t reliant on forced sales during intermittent production, and provides fuel that ensures clean, resilient power even during lulls in renewable energy.

1907. ID: 4785
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Mira Wenzel, Philipp Godron, Simon Müller (all from Agora Energiewende), Dominik Huebler, and Leonie Janisch (both from NERA Economic Consulting).
   Statement: We believe that the creation of an Offshore Bidding Zone (OBZ) for the Danish Energy Island projects will lead to lower revenues for wind farm operators, as the price within the OBZ matches the price of the bidding zone where capacity remains available. However, this results in higher congestion revenues for grid users or grid operators. Depending on whether grid operators are allowed to retain these congestion revenues or are required to return them to grid users after exceeding a regulated return, the incentives for sizing the grid connection vary significantly.

The Danish Energy Agency has justified the establishment of a new price zone to address structural bottlenecks that would otherwise arise between the Energy Island and Zealand within the same bidding zone (DK2). Bidders for future offshore wind power projects in this region must consider the uncertainties and complexities related to expected revenues, as these will influence their bids starting in 2024.

Energinet's simulation suggests that the expected price differences due to the new price zone will be minimal. However, with increasing cross-border interconnections, several regulatory and economic challenges must be addressed.

1927. ID: 4354
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: Dan Jørgensen
   Statement: The establishment of Energiø Bornholm, Denmark's first energy island, will require significant investment, including a 245 km direct current connection between Bornholm and Zealand and two 400 kW converter stations on Bornholm and Zealand. This project, part of an agreement with Germany to link the energy island to the German electricity grid, will cost Denmark approximately 13.9 billion kroner. This amount is a reduction from the initial 16.9 billion kroner estimate due to the shared financial responsibilities with Germany.

The cost of 13.9 billion kroner will be distributed among Denmark's 3.3 million electricity customers through electricity tariffs over time, amounting to an average of 4,200 kroner per customer. Payments will not be collected through direct invoices but will instead be integrated into ongoing electricity tariffs managed by Energinet, which oversees the operation and expansion of Denmark's electricity grid.

Energiø Bornholm is expected to deliver a capacity of 3 gigawatts, equivalent to the output of 200 offshore wind turbines, each rated at 15 megawatts. While the project adds costs, Energinet is working to mitigate the impact on electricity tariffs. In 2022, Energinet allocated 1.2 billion kroner to improve international electricity connections and plans to return 1.6 billion kroner to consumers through tariff reductions, which will help lower electricity prices.

This project is critical to Denmark's green energy transition and the broader European energy network, ensuring long-term sustainability and energy security despite the initial costs to electricity customers.

The Energy Island Bornholm project lacks economic justification, as concluded by analysis firm Kraka. Senior economist Frederik Læssøe Nielsen from Kraka has publicly requested a single strong argument for establishing the Energy Island Bornholm, noting that the project faces so many challenges that it no longer makes sense:
- 💰 A minimum of 31.5 billion DKK in state subsidies, according to the Danish Energy Agency.
- 🔌 Adding more wind turbines in the Baltic Sea does not improve energy security.
- 💧 Producing PtX on Bornholm would be extremely expensive, as it is cheaper to produce PtX using other energy sources than offshore wind.

At Kärnfull, we have long questioned the excessively expensive energy island projects. In contrast, nuclear power can deliver cheap and stable electricity and hydrogen without requiring industrialization of natural areas. 

Kärnfull Next is already developing nuclear projects in Sweden and is interested in doing the same in Denmark if the ban on nuclear power is lifted. Nuclear power would eliminate the need for large-scale energy islands by providing stable production of electricity, district heating, and hydrogen. By locating nuclear power plants at existing power plant sites, we can avoid further industrializing nature. 

Additionally, many of our customers have saved significant amounts of money by switching to electricity contracts with 100% nuclear power, avoiding overpriced fixed-rate plans or hidden fees. Nuclear power offers a practical, economical, and sustainable energy solution for Denmark.

1988. ID: 4019
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Helle Østergaard Kristiansen
   Statement: I’ve often said that European energy policy is like a slow-motion train wreck. While many see the EU as a leader in the green transition and the energy transformation, the reality isn’t as rosy as it may seem. From my position at Danske Commodities, an energy trading company specializing in electricity, gas, and renewable energy, I’m at the center of what I describe as this train wreck.

One of the biggest challenges is that renewable energy, like wind and solar, doesn’t always align with demand. The wind doesn’t always blow, and the sun doesn’t always shine—especially not when there’s a football match on TV. This means we need to take energy from where there’s an excess and send it to where there’s a shortage. That sounds simple, but it’s far from it.

We’re heading into a challenging period. The electrification of society is crucial for the environment and climate, and it’s absolutely the right direction to go. But the problem lies in how energy is physically moved around on the energy grid—both within Denmark and across borders. Think of it like transporting goods on highways. Right now, our energy “highways” aren’t sufficiently developed, creating enormous bottlenecks.

For example, sometimes Denmark produces so much wind energy that we can’t even transport it to Germany because the grid isn’t robust enough to handle the volume. And this problem is only exacerbated by our inability to store the energy we produce. Without proper storage, we can’t save excess energy for times when production is low.

These challenges are real and significant, and if we don’t address them, the green transition could face serious hurdles despite our best intentions.

1999. ID: 2864
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Strategy and planning
   Actor: Laila Kildesgaard, Maja Bendtsen
   Statement: The development plan for Bornholm's electricity grid from 2025 is open for public input. With electrification accelerating, electricity consumption on Bornholm is expected to more than double by 2030, driven by the adoption of heat pumps for home heating and electric vehicles for private and commercial transport. Investments in the grid are necessary to accommodate this growth, including upgrades to infrastructure, IT systems, and measurement equipment, estimated to require approximately 500 million DKK over the next five years. 

The existing grid, built for a different era, must evolve to support not only traditional household needs but also heating and transport electrification. Legally, all customers are entitled to sufficient electricity supply, and the investment plan reflects this obligation. Transparency regarding investment needs and calculations is critical, as these directly affect consumers and prices.

The plan also considers the potential integration of Bornholm's grid with the future Energy Island and transformer station south of Aakirkeby. Currently, Bornholm remains connected to the state grid via the submarine cable from Hasle, and any changes to this connection will be addressed in the next grid development plan in 2027.

We strongly encourage large energy consumers on Bornholm—such as the municipality, municipal companies, major state enterprises, the hospital, and large private businesses like metalworking companies, dairies, and slaughterhouses—to contribute to the consultation process. Their insights into changes in electricity consumption or investment plans could significantly impact grid investment needs. 

Private individuals and local experts are also invited to share knowledge to refine electricity consumption forecasts. The proposed development plan for Trefor El-net Øst is available for review on the Danish Utility Regulator's website from April 4, 2024, with the consultation period running until May 1, 2024.

2017. ID: 3036
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Jan Vejnaa-Hansen
   Statement: I want to make it clear that the current efforts to develop green energy facilities like Power-to-X will not meet the expectations we have for climate impact. There is a disconnect between political ambitions and actual feasibility.  

Take, for example, Mette Frederiksen’s 2023 New Year’s speech, where she promised CO2-neutral fuel for all domestic flights by 2030 and the first fossil-free route by 2025. Either the Prime Minister has been misinformed, or these are overly ambitious election promises. Based on my analysis, Power-to-X is so inefficient that even using all the electricity generated from the wind farm ‘Middelgrunden,’ we could only keep a single domestic flight operational for 20% of a day. To supply all flights operating to and from Copenhagen Airport with hydrogen- and CO2-based aviation fuel, we would need 2,600 wind farms of that size.  

The same inefficiencies apply to hydrogen-powered cars. Producing liquid hydrogen for these vehicles using wind energy results in up to 84% of the energy being wasted on processes other than transport itself. By contrast, electric cars waste only 23% of their energy, making hydrogen impractical and unsound for land transport.  

As for maritime transport, the industry does not expect CO2-based fuels to surpass fossil fuels until 2050, largely relying on biomethanol. However, biomethanol is also difficult to produce in sufficient quantities. These realities highlight why the current path for green energy transition faces critical challenges.

2018. ID: 3040
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Financial viability and (un)profitability
   Actor: Lars Aagaard
   Statement: In 2020, when the previous government made the initial agreement on the energy islands, it was assumed that the offshore wind turbines would not only be self-financing but also cover the cost of the necessary electricity infrastructure. However, in our assessment last year, we found that offshore wind alone couldn't cover these costs. Consequently, it was politically agreed that there would be investment willingness in the project corresponding to the infrastructure costs of 17.6 billion. At the same time, it was still assumed that the offshore wind turbines should be able to sustain themselves. But whether this assumption holds true will only be known once the tender process is complete.

The agreed state support – and thus the taxpayer cost – of 17.6 billion must be weighed against the benefits for electricity consumers, including lower electricity prices and increased supply security, due to the large amounts of new wind power entering the grid.

As for the gap between the estimated support need of 31.5 billion and the politically approved support of 17.6 billion, the truth will only be revealed once the large tender process is concluded. There is a possibility that market actors may state that they cannot build the offshore wind turbines without support, which could result in no bids. However, there are also price scenarios that suggest it could be attractive. We will test this in the market, and the outcome of the tender will determine this discussion.

If no bids come in because the terms, including the support framework, are unattractive to companies, I would then discuss the situation with the political coalition. I cannot speculate further until we have new input from the tender process or Energinet’s preparatory work.

Regarding the timeline for the tender, I am committed to it happening as quickly as possible, but I do not have any updates on the schedule.

If, back in 2020, we had known that the energy islands would not be profitable and would require support for the North Sea Energy Island of 50 billion and for Bornholm Energy Island of over 30 billion, would the projects have been politically scrapped? That’s a counterfactual question, but it’s easy to imagine that at the time, the political decisions seemed more straightforward when it was expected that the projects could proceed without support. However, decisions must always be made based on the information available at the time.

Did we make poor decisions based on the available information in 2020? I wasn’t involved, so I can’t judge. In hindsight, it’s always much easier to be wise.

2019. ID: 3045
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Claire Bergaentzlé
   Statement: No developers submitted bids for Denmark's largest-ever offshore wind auction, putting Denmark's renewable energy future at risk. This outcome, while not entirely surprising, stems from several critical issues:

The projects expose developers to full market risks at a time when raw material costs are extremely high. The government has imposed severe financial penalties for any delays in grid connections. Developers must bear the full cost burden of building connection lines to the grid under the deep connection setup. Additionally, Denmark's state co-ownership rule requires developers to give up 20% of project value to the state.

These challenges create cascading effects that threaten multiple strategic initiatives. The 3GW Bornholm Energy Island project may now struggle to secure financing. Denmark will likely miss its renewable energy targets. The country's goal of developing 4-6 GW of electrolysis capacity by 2030 is in serious jeopardy, especially given the transmission system operator's recent announcement of major delays in constructing the Denmark-Germany hydrogen pipeline.

Unless the Danish government implements strong supportive measures, both offshore wind development and hydrogen infrastructure ambitions are at serious risk of failure. This represents a critical turning point for Denmark's entire renewable energy strategy.

2028. ID: 2522
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)

   Statement: We understand that the people of Bornholm want to benefit from the advantages the Energy Island brings, both in terms of green electricity consumption and production on the island. I am pleased that our analysis shows it is technically feasible and a good solution from a socioeconomic perspective. However, it does not work in a way that Bornholm residents will have lower electricity prices simply because the island hosts the Energy Island. 

We have been accustomed to stable electricity prices across Denmark until the war in Ukraine caused significant fluctuations and increases. As part of the Energy Island project, we are introducing what is called a 'third bidding zone,' which acts as a trading market for the electricity produced and sold on Bornholm. When we connect the Energy Island to the local grid, residents will gain access to locally produced electricity. This setup ensures relatively stable prices without major fluctuations. 

Additionally, Bornholm’s location between Denmark and Germany, which generally have similar electricity prices, combined with the island’s excellent wind conditions, contributes to a stable and reliable electricity supply.

2036. ID: 2598
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Andreas Skriver Hansen, Jesper Manniche, Karin Topsø Larsen;
   Statement: Our research on Bornholm and the Energy Island project reveals critical insights about local community transitions in large-scale energy projects. These projects require fundamental changes to the entire social ecosystem, not just technical infrastructure.
Local communities must be treated as a crucial development front. The Energy Island project demands multiple complex structural changes at the local level, including:
- Creating visions that reflect local realities
- Developing new business and education strategies
- Protecting local interests
- Coordinating across different administrative levels
- Implementing new physical planning procedures
- Establishing comprehensive local engagement plans
- Executing ambitious communication strategies
While Bornholm may have advantages due to Denmark's leadership in green transition and the Energy Island initiative, Bornholm's experience offers valuable lessons for other regions. The findings from Bornholm can inform similar offshore wind projects across Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea region.
To ensure successful and just transitions, we need systematic collective efforts to compare and learn from these projects. More theoretical and empirical research is needed since there is currently no blueprint for managing local transition processes. The Bornholm case demonstrates how different places, each with unique socio-spatial, techno-economic, and political configurations, can position themselves in the emerging energy transition landscape where centralization and peripheralization will create different opportunities for competing locations.

2044. ID: 2709
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: Waste of tax payer’s money
   Actor: Poul Blicher Andersen
   Statement: The economics of the Energy Island project are highly questionable. My cost-benefit analysis indicates that this project could result in a loss of 48 to 77 billion Danish kroner over its lifetime for electricity customers and the state treasury. This substantial deficit is due to a significant mismatch between the costs of producing electricity from the Energy Island and the expected selling price of that electricity.

Furthermore, the projected return on investment for this project is inadequate. The Danish Energy Agency estimates a 4% return, which is far too low to attract investors to such a high-risk venture. The energy market is notoriously unpredictable, and no one can accurately forecast electricity prices 20 years into the future. This uncertainty, combined with the low projected returns, makes the Energy Island project an unattractive investment proposition.

Given these economic realities, I would strongly caution against proceeding with the Energy Island project in its current form. The potential financial risks and burdens on Danish consumers and taxpayers are simply too great to ignore.

2049. ID: 3048
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Peter Frohböse
   Statement: I, Peter Frohböse think that the potential of the Baltic Sea for offshore wind energy is severely underestimated. I believe the opportunities in the region are much greater than the goals set by the surrounding countries. Compared to the North Sea, the offshore areas in the Baltic Sea are closer to the coast. Additionally, the Baltic Sea is shallower and has good soil conditions in many areas, which results in lower project costs than those of the North Sea. However, due to slightly lower wind speeds, the energy yield is somewhat smaller. Despite this, the levelized cost of energy for offshore wind farms is similar to that of the North Sea. The specific location of the wind farm plays a significant role in determining the cost.

Regarding the ice in the Baltic Sea, it is not an unsolvable problem, but it requires adequate time and expertise during project planning. What concerns me more is the patchwork of state-specific auction mechanisms, regulations, and guidelines across the region.

The Baltic Sea is in global competition for offshore wind energy development. Wind parks are being built all over the world, and there is currently a shortage of suppliers, which means the demand for new wind parks exceeds the capacities of suppliers and developers. As a result, companies are consolidating their portfolios and focusing on the most attractive markets. While the Baltic Sea has significant potential, it is divided among eight countries, each with its own regulations and mechanisms. Companies may therefore prefer to focus on a larger market elsewhere in the world or in the North Sea. The solution to this could be the creation of EU-wide standards and harmonization between countries.

Regarding the supply chain shortage, it is generally more difficult for new companies to enter the market. New entrants would need time for product development, but in the meantime, they would struggle to compete on price with established companies. Higher prices are not feasible because offshore wind farms are planned based on current market prices, which would make them unprofitable. Therefore, I expect existing players to expand their production capacities. Opportunities for new market participants exist for suppliers of components and parts (2nd and 3rd-tier suppliers), such as turbine manufacturers. Additionally, there is a significant opportunity for financial service providers to enter the market.

2055. ID: 3295
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Youtube user
   Statement: What frustrates me the most is the constant omission of external costs associated with wind and solar energy. It's fine when small amounts of wind and solar energy are integrated into the market. However, as their share grows, other energy sources become more expensive. For instance, biogas plants can only operate profitably for 12 hours a day instead of 24 hours. There are also long-term storage costs to consider. With sufficient baseload power, only minimal energy storage is needed, such as with lithium-iron-phosphate batteries. If we calculate one kilowatt-hour of storage for 24 hours with a 20-year lifespan and a cost of €80 per kilowatt-hour, the storage cost per kilowatt of stochastic energy generation would be approximately 1.1 cents. This isn't noticeable under current electricity costs, especially when only a fraction of energy is generated stochastically. 

But what happens if, in the future, we rely almost entirely on wind and solar energy and need to store energy for 10 days? Storage costs could reach around 10 cents per kilowatt-hour, on top of the 3-8 cents for generation costs. In that scenario, it would be better to keep nuclear power plants operational and only expand wind and solar energy to a level that doesn't disrupt residential areas or nature reserves.

2078. ID: 3109
   Year: 2024
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Duvivier, Alban J. F.; Cutululis, Nicolaos A.; Saborío-Romano, Oscar; Randewijk, Peter Jan; Yang, Li
   Statement: The Danish "Energy Island" project, with its multi-terminal HVDC grid model, presents a viable approach for integrating significant amounts of offshore wind power. This study investigates energy dissipation strategies in such systems, particularly focusing on a 4GW HVDC-MT grid designed to connect Belgium, Denmark, and the Danish North Sea Energy Island (DNSEI) by 2032. The primary challenge is energy dissipation, especially with the substantial increase in wind power generation anticipated for the future.

The key technology investigated in this paper is the use of **wind turbine DC-link choppers**. These choppers are essential for ensuring that the system can handle faults not only at the wind turbine terminals but also in the onshore AC grid. The study compared the performance of WT-DC link choppers with two other energy dissipation technologies: onshore HVDC choppers and offshore AC systems. These technologies were tested under different fault conditions-AC onshore, DC offshore, and AC offshore-focusing on voltage fluctuations and the necessary chopper capacities for fault ride-through.

The findings indicate that the best performance in terms of voltage stabilization is achieved through a combination of WT-DC choppers and HVDC choppers. Specifically, turbines equipped with DC-link choppers can address offshore fault ride-through, making AC choppers unnecessary due to their similar performance. For onshore faults, HVDC choppers help manage temporary voltage overshoot by dissipating power first, followed by WT choppers. This process requires offshore wind farms to operate in a grid-forming mode, where offshore converters regulate the power transfer.

However, this study is based on a proof of concept using first principles and does not account for the costs or operational considerations that would be involved in implementing such a dissipation strategy. A comprehensive cost-benefit analysis would be essential before any real-world application of these strategies in wind turbine economics and grid operation.

   Statement: I suggest that Denmark uses an auction format called CfD (Contracts for Difference). In this system, companies would have the opportunity to request a guaranteed minimum price for the electricity they produce. The funds can be raised by adding a surcharge to the electricity price paid by consumers. Conversely, energy companies would pay money back to the state if the price exceeds the agreed minimum.

This system could be designed so that politicians set a total cap on the amount of money wind companies can receive, ensuring that the minimum price is not paid when there is a negative electricity price, meaning when the wind turbines are not needed.

However, it is not only the electricity supply that politicians need to oversee and support. Politicians should also take ownership of demand. The market, in the form of private investors, is not capable of handling this, in my opinion.

This includes, among other things, a faster and more comprehensive electrification of industry and society. Politicians hold the power to make this happen.

2126. ID: 99
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: Job creation and innovation
   Actor: Claus M. Andersen
   Statement: The Second Life for Powerplants project may be the most groundbreaking initiative we have hosted in the 15 years Bornholms Energi & Forsyning has been involved in research and demonstration projects. The combined heat and power plant on Skansevej in Rønne will soon house this initiative, which brings together European pioneers in energy technology to address the greatest challenge in the sustainable transition: capturing and storing solar and wind energy to ensure power and heat availability on cloudy, low-wind days. 

With a budget of 100 million DKK, including 60 million DKK in EU funding, the project aims to repurpose the original technology of power plants and build on the existing expertise of their employees. This includes reusing steam turbines, generators, control systems, and connections to the electricity and district heating networks. The plant will integrate three innovative storage technologies: a salt storage system, used electric vehicle batteries, and a high-tech flywheel battery. At the heart of the concept is advanced control software designed to ensure a continuous supply of heat and electricity, even on cloudy, windless days.

This project will provide invaluable insights into managing and storing solar and wind energy, maintaining balance in the electricity system, and determining the investments needed to fully phase out oil and reduce the reliance on wood chips. It will demonstrate how we can make maximum use of solar and wind power without significantly increasing costs for Bornholm residents.

Furthermore, the experiences gained on Bornholm can be easily replicated elsewhere, such as converting a Polish coal plant into a flexible energy storage facility for solar and wind power. Hosting such a project on Bornholm suggests we may need to raise expectations regarding the additional activities the Energy Island Bornholm will bring to the region.

The North Sea also has stronger winds and far fewer bird migration routes, making it perfect for offshore wind farms. The North Sea's areas are enormous compared to the waters south of Bornholm, allowing for the placement of 40 times more wind turbines.  

I believe Energiø Nordsøen is approximately 40 times more important to realize than Energiø Bornholm. Therefore, Energiø Nordsøen must be built first and as quickly as possible.  

Move Energiø Bornholm to the North Sea and spare Bornholm and its surrounding waters from industrial energy development.  

Why has Energiø Nordsøen been stopped? It seems almost surreal!  

It is deeply concerning that Energinet can expropriate land—or threaten to do so—for a project that is partially financed by Germany.  

If justice prevails, projects that are wholly or partially funded by foreign states or large international companies should not be allowed to use § 73 of the Danish Constitution concerning expropriation. Danish courts, and possibly the EU courts, should investigate this matter.

2203. ID: 1906
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: German collaboration
   Actor: Energinet
   Statement: Our analyses reveal that the Bornholm Energy Island’s electricity infrastructure becomes significantly more cost-effective when power from the wind farms is transmitted to both Denmark and Germany, rather than just to Denmark. Over the 30-year lifespan of the project, this approach is expected to deliver a substantial net benefit, estimated in the nine-figure range, compared to a solution without a connection to Germany.

It’s important to note that these calculations involve a considerable degree of uncertainty, as they rely on assumptions that are not yet fully established. As part of our assessment, we focus on the standalone economic value of the electricity infrastructure, which enables power from the Bornholm Energy Island to connect to electricity markets in one or more countries. While the cost-benefit analysis accounts for the value of the wind power generated, it does not include the costs associated with constructing the wind farms themselves.

We recommend making electrical connections to both Denmark and Germany from the Bornholm Energy Island, with two possible time schedules in mind.

Two time schedules make it possible to fulfill the political goal of establishing offshore wind power at the Bornholm Energy Island before 2030, even if it proves not to be possible for the foreign partner to establish their connection to the energy island in time.

We therefore recommend:

TIME SCHEDULE 1: We, in cooperation with German TSO 50Hertz, establish via the Bornholm Energy Island a 1.2 GW electrical connection between Zealand and Bornholm, and a 2 GW connection between Bornholm and Germany. All onshore and offshore electrical installations and interconnections between countries are ready for operation by the first half of 2029.

Or:

TIME SCHEDULE 2: We establish a 1.2 GW electrical connection between Zealand and the Bornholm Energy Island, which together with electrical installations in Denmark are ready for operation at the beginning of 2029. At the same time, we and 50Hertz work jointly towards an expected future 2 GW interconnection between Bornholm and Germany, ready for operation in 2030 or as soon as possible thereafter.

2212. ID: 2304
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: TenneT
   Statement: We, at TenneT, have calculated that it is possible to build the energy island ""at social cost."" While the construction of such an island is more expensive compared to conventional infrastructure, especially when the islands are located further from the coast, we anticipate savings because the cables can immediately serve as international power connections. We refer to this as the ""wheel-and-spoke"" system, which ensures that the new energy infrastructure remains efficient in the future.  

As offshore wind capacity in the North Sea reaches 180 gigawatts, we believe that power exchange between countries will be essential. The islands will function as relays, collecting power from surrounding turbines and transmitting it to land. By laying cables to countries like the Netherlands and Germany, we can facilitate power transport between nations at the same time.  

This cross-border power exchange is necessary because turbines don’t generate power consistently. For example, there are times when there is no wind or turbines require maintenance, meaning that about half of the time, the cable from the island to the mainland is underutilized. By using the cable for international power transport, we can increase its usage time to 80%, improving the cable's efficiency and accelerating its return on investment. Furthermore, this reduces the need for long cables for each turbine or turbine group.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Since Energinet's "Business Case" from 2022, expectations for the project's economic benefits to society have significantly deteriorated. Therefore, a decision needs to be made whether to modify or abandon the project.

The choice of an energy island instead of a platform solution leads to concentrated energy conversions in few points, thereby increasing the vulnerability of electricity supply in Denmark and the rest of Europe. In light of increased international tensions, this choice should be reevaluated.

The technical interconnection on the energy island is described as "immature" in Energinet's risk assessment. This is an understatement, as the interconnection is challenging and has only been attempted at full scale in very few places worldwide.

No Danish companies develop or produce HVDC equipment, so Denmark has no interest in betting on unproven solutions. Multi-terminal offshore HVDC solutions should not be included in the project in any form until the necessary new technologies have been fully tested elsewhere.

Analyses of alternative solutions have been neglected. Due to poor economics and technological uncertainty, the project should be suspended until all relevant solutions have been properly investigated and evaluated.

2226. ID: 5919
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: Energy hubs towards P2X
   Actor: Technical University of Denmark
   Statement: Denmark has set ambitious goals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 70% by 2030 and to become independent of fossil fuels by 2050. To achieve these goals, Denmark plans to accelerate the decarbonization of the energy system by replacing coal- and gas-fired power plants with renewable energy sources. Offshore wind, together with onshore wind and solar, will form the foundation of electricity production in a decarbonized system.  

Denmark is already a world leader in wind power and plans to install an additional 6.8 GW of offshore wind capacity by 2030, quadrupling the existing capacity of 1.7 GW. To enable the cost-effective integration of such large volumes of offshore wind into the power grid, the Danish Parliament decided in 2020 to develop and construct two energy islands: one on Bornholm in the Baltic Sea and another as an artificial island in the North Sea.  

These projects are highly ambitious, particularly the North Sea energy island, which will become one of Europe’s largest energy hubs, with a long-term goal of installing 10 GW of offshore wind—twice the capacity of the largest power plants today. The construction of the two energy islands by 2033 represents a 'Mars mission' for Denmark's energy system.  

This mission faces three key challenges. First, there is a significant gap between current cost-effective technologies and the technologies required to realize the vision for the energy islands. Second, new public/private sector operational models are needed to design, plan, construct, and operate the islands cost-effectively and reliably. Third, the energy islands will serve as laboratories for the transformation required in the energy system as Denmark—and the world—move toward 100% fossil fuel independence by 2050.  

A specific challenge in the development of the energy islands is designing and building electrical infrastructure capable of handling a variable electricity supply based entirely on renewable energy. Each energy island will function as an 'electron metropolis,' where electrons, driven by the kinetic energy of offshore wind, move through power cables, are traded on markets by multiple suppliers, and eventually reach the mainland. From there, they will either be delivered directly to consumers or used in power-to-X systems to split molecules. These electron metropolises must operate with millisecond precision to manage production, trading, and transmission of several gigawatts of electricity, requiring the development and maturation of entirely new solutions. This represents a significant challenge that is not yet widely recognized.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2231. ID: 5695
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: DI.Paul Schöpf
   Statement: The concept of energy islands is crucial for ensuring the autonomous energy supply of Germany and the EU in the near future. While the Danish energy island project in the North Sea faces delays and significant concerns, such as the destruction of fish spawning grounds and uncertainties about rising sea levels, there is a better alternative: floating energy islands.

Floating energy islands can be constructed using a durable, coated timber-hybrid material combined with a modular, high-load-bearing platform design. These structures can be protected by wave breakers also made from timber. Submerged timber caissons filled with sand are placed on the seabed, and reinforcement grids attached to the walls are set under a weak electric current. Within weeks, bio-rock forms on the timber panels, creating a new artificial reef. This reef not only protects the floating energy island but also enhances the underwater ecosystem, safeguarding it from storm surges and high waves. Crucially, this design adapts to rising sea levels, ensuring long-term functionality.

Floating energy islands offer additional advantages, including the direct storage of offshore wind energy in the high gigawatt-hour range. With this stored energy, the islands can support the production and storage of hydrogen, ammonia, and even freshwater using installed facilities. These floating platforms can also serve as large refueling and supply hubs in the open sea. They are cost-effective, faster to implement, and can be modified or dismantled as needed.

This floating solution aligns with nature, minimizes ecological disruption, and provides a flexible and sustainable approach to offshore energy development.

2243. ID: 3870
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Melanie Markwick-Day
   Statement: Meshed offshore grid projects face unique challenges related to the cost and complexity of installing and maintaining HVDC infrastructure, which is essential for creating meshed offshore grids. While HVDC cables are more economical than HVAC cables over long distances, the high upfront costs of equipment, such as terminal converter stations, and the volatile price of copper add significant financial barriers. Furthermore, the scarcity of cable-laying vessels—only about 40 globally—combined with supply chain constraints and a lack of trained professionals skilled in HVDC installation and maintenance, further complicates the process.

Modernizing the grid also requires digitalization, which offers benefits such as improved demand response and greater energy storage capacity. However, it introduces risks, including increased vulnerability to cyberattacks and potential damage from physical attacks by malicious actors, a risk that will grow as deep-sea exploration technology advances.

Natural and accidental damage to subsea cables is another significant concern. Underwater earthquakes, landslides, and hydrodynamic scour can reshape the seabed and harm infrastructure. Additional risks include damage from remotely operated vehicles used in research, fishing gear, and boat anchors. These challenges collectively emphasize the need for careful planning, investment, and risk mitigation to ensure the viability and resilience of meshed offshore grids.

We have outlined three key bottom lines for Energy Island Bornholm:  

1️⃣ **Climate Impact**: The project will displace 3 million tons of CO2 annually and, more importantly, pave the way for additional energy islands, which are crucial for the EU's green transition.  

2️⃣ **Industrial Policy**: Bornholm, as an existing island, is the ideal test platform for future energy islands. This will provide Danish companies with a significant innovation advantage in developing energy island technologies.  

3️⃣ **Security Policy**: Energy Island Bornholm, with its combination of electricity trade connections and large amounts of green energy, is a vital step toward reducing the EU's dependence on Russian energy. While the project is significant as one of the largest climate initiatives ever, its greatest impact lies in paving the way for additional energy islands, which are critical for Europe to become energy self-sufficient.  

Additionally, we argue that the project has a strong chance of being a good economic investment for Denmark. Current calculations show a negative social economy of 4 billion DKK. However, this is due to challenges in fully accounting for the project's many benefits, particularly its innovative aspects, in the Danish Energy Agency's calculations.

2270. ID: 4416
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Steffen W. Frølund
   Statement: I have proposed decision proposal B91 to the Danish Parliament, suggesting that the government establish a commission to investigate the potential use of nuclear power in Denmark’s energy supply.  

Denmark requires significant amounts of renewable energy from wind and solar, which Liberal Alliance fully supports. However, it is impossible to build a reliable energy system solely on wind and solar due to their inherent fluctuations. For example, a cloudy, windless Christmas Eve could leave households without adequate energy supply. As Denmark increases its reliance on wind and solar, these fluctuations will only become more pronounced, making it essential to balance the energy system.  

Currently, the plan is to store surplus energy generated on sunny and windy days using Power-to-X technology or various types of batteries and to utilize gas boilers when renewable energy production is low. While these stabilizing measures are important, there are alternative ways to create stable, green baseload energy. The goal must be an abundance of affordable green electricity.  

Nuclear power is an unavoidable component of Europe’s energy future. Many countries already use nuclear power, are expanding its use, or regret reducing their reliance on it. Denmark, however, actively prohibits nuclear power despite importing it from other countries.  

Unfortunately, Denmark’s debate on nuclear power is clouded by historical prejudices and misinformation. I aim to challenge and correct these misconceptions, enabling an informed discussion about the potential role of nuclear energy in Denmark’s green transition.

2275. ID: 6428
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: German collaboration
   Actor: 50Hertz Transmission GmbH
   Statement: We have signed a contract for the manufacturing and installation of 3,500 kilometers of 525 kV HVDC cables, including onshore and offshore cables for the German grid connection of the Bornholm Energy Island. Danish company NKT has been awarded the contract.

The cable system will span a total of 164 kilometers, with 149 kilometers being offshore cables. The system will include two cable cores and an additional metallic return, amounting to a total of 492 kilometers of cables. The subsea cables will connect to the existing grid at the shoreline in Lubmin county.

This planned connection, with a transmission capacity of 2,000 MW, is a crucial component of the joint project with Energinet to deliver green energy efficiently.

   Statement: We follow a support model at UNIDO that adheres to a comprehensive list of quality requirements for the Centres. We ensure our approach is demand-driven, involving local and international stakeholders early in the design phase. We prioritize strong ownership from regional counterparts and the host country, including their financial and in-kind contributions. Additionally, we ensure the Centres effectively respond to country-specific needs through a Network of National Focal Institutions (NFIs). 

Our “form follows function” principle ensures a small initial staff base that can grow in line with mobilized funding and projects. The Centres are equipped to mobilize grants and are staffed with qualified local and international professionals. We maintain an internal quality, appraisal, and management framework while focusing on establishing long-term flagship programmes.    Statement: I am Wenxin Yang, and I believe that international collaboration is essential for the global transition to sustainable energy. Denmark, with its extensive experience in green energy, can serve as a valuable source of knowledge for other countries, including China. 
While acknowledging Denmark's pioneering role, China should develop its own unique approach to achieving carbon neutrality by 2060, tailored to its specific national conditions. 
I believe in clean energy systems and optimization strategies within the framework of ENSYSCO, a technology based on power-to-x. I am confident that this approach can provide a viable pathway for China to achieve carbon neutrality while ensuring the efficient and secure integration of sustainable energy into its power grid.

2304. ID: 835
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: Ina Jakobsen
   Statement: I Ina Jakobsen, a student at the University of Oslo/University of Aalborg, believe that wind energy projects have a significant impact on society, and vice versa. 
To understand this complex relationship better, future research should focus on comparative studies that analyze how different societies shape the development and implementation of wind energy technology, and how these projects, in turn, transform those societies. 
For successful wind energy projects, fostering a sense of ownership among the local community is crucial. When people feel they have a stake in the project, can influence its outcomes, and potentially benefit economically, it leads to increased social acceptance and a higher likelihood of project success. 
Furthermore, the creation of social capital, which refers to the networks and relationships within a community, should be a key consideration in the planning and execution of wind energy projects.

2305. ID: 969
   Year: 2025
   Cluster: (None)
   Actor: AVK Group
   Statement: We at AVK UK and AVK Donkin are involved in the H100 project, where we are supplying S310 Flow Limitors to a test network that uses 100% hydrogen. These limitors are critical for securing the network in the event of a pipe burst, as they automatically cut off the supply to prevent accidents.

For us at AVK, embracing the future in power-to-x means being able to confirm and document that our products meet the increasing demands of this industry. This includes conducting type tests on our products to ensure they are fit for the task. We have worked closely with FORCE Technology to develop a valve test specifically designed for hydrogen use.
